Course Rationale:

Constitution is the basic law of the land for any nation, and it is expected for its citizens to have
knowledge of it. This course aims to ingrain into the student’s mind the basic principles of Constitution of
India. Students are already exposed to Preamble of the constitution, but the exposure is only superficial.
This course aims at providing in depth rationale behind the Preamble. It also aims to provide knowledge
with respect to fundamental rights provided in the Constitution and permissible restrictions upon it and the
institutions within ‘State’ and their inter-relation with each other. Topics covered in this course consists of
the evolution and nature of the Indian Constitution, Preamble, Fundamental rights and duties, Directive
Principles of State Policy, the Union Parliament, Federal structure of Indian polity, Indian Judiciary,
Emergency provisions and Amendment powers and its usage since inception of Constitution till date.

Course Objectives:

1. To enable the students to understand the principles mentioned in our Constitution and apply them in
regular course of activities, personal or professional.

2. To enable them to know the structure of Indian polity, legal framework and inter-relations of
institutions of ‘State’ in India

Course Outcomes:

After completion of the course, students would be able to:

1. Understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and to understand the
principles mentioned in its Preamble.

2. Inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions upon it so as to
enjoy these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously performing their duties and concept
of Directive Principles of State policy and to apply these principles into their professional lives.

3. Ingrain the structure of our polity and inter-relation of various organs of State — Legislature
(Parliament), Executive (Government) and Judiciary (Courts) and also relation between Union, States
and Local Self Governments and amendment of the Constitution by the Parliament.

4. Attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know the additional
powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to understand the Amendment
procedure.

Unit | Description Duration

i. Introduction 3
Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as
Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental
differences between science and engineering by drawing a
comparison between eye and camera, Bird flying and aircraft.
Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an independent
scientific discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss how
biological observations of 18th Century that lead to major
discoveries. Examples from Brownian motion and the origin of
thermodynamics by referring to the original observation of Robert
Brown and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight the
fundamental importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.

2, Classification
Convey that classification per se is not what biology is all about. 6
The underlying criterion, such as morphological, biochemical or
ecological be highlighted. Hierarchy of life forms at

heterotrophs, lithotropes (d) Ammonia excretion - aminotelic,
uricoteliec, ureotelic (e) Habitata- acquatic or terrestrial (e)
Molecular taxonomy- three major kingdoms of life. A given

classification. Model organisms for the study of biology come from

Physical Sciences” Mendel’s laws, Concept of segregation and
independent assortment. Concept of allele. Gene mapping, Gene
interaction, Epistasis. Meiosis and Mitosis be taught as a part of
genetics. Emphasis to be give not to the mechanics of cell division
nor the phases but how genetic material passes from parent to
offspring. Concepts of recessiveness and dominance. Concept of
mapping of phenotype to genes. Discuss about the single gene
disorders in humans.

Discuss the concept of complementation using human genetics.

Biomolecules

Convey that all forms of life has the same building blocks and yet
the manifestations are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of
life. In this context discuss monomeric units and polymeric
structures. Discuss about sugars, starch and cellulose. Amino acids
and proteins. Nucleotides and DNA/RNA. Two carbon units and
lipids.

Convey that without catalysis life would not have existed on earth
Enzymology: How to monitor enzyme catalyzed reactions. How
does an enzyme catalyzereactions. Enzyme classification.

Information Transfer

The molecular basis of coding and decoding genetic information is
universal Molecular basis of information transfer. DNA as a

stranded to double helix to nucleosomes. Concept of genetic code.
Universality and degeneracy of genetic code. Define gene in terms

Objectives:
 To sensitize students about criticality of operations function in a business organization.
 To impart students with the knowledge on various operations management issues and equip
them with skills to analyze them with effective corrective action and implementation.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Use basic operations function, operations management and productivity related to operations
and formulate operations strategy in organizations.
2. Recognize the processes, their types, layouts, process analysis and their applications and
undertake a detailed study on selection of suitable locations for manufacturing plants,
facilities and service centers.
3. Understand different production system with their advantages and disadvantages along with
a learning on Product-Process Matrix and job sequencing and scheduling methods.
4. Undertake a detailed study and learning of Inventory management systems and different
inventory control models with their applications.
5. Implement Quality Management, TQM concepts in an organization and appreciate Just in
Time (JIT), Six Sigma, Lean Production and Quality Function Deployment and their
applications and understand of Theory of Constraints.

Objectives:
 With Innovation being an imperative for any organization to maintain its leadership in
the highly competitive environment, it is important for all Business owners and future
employees of the organizations to understand the all-important concepts & processes
related to Innovation.
 The course is essentially about building and sustaining innovation within organizations
by creating an innovative and learning organization. It aims to focus on innovation
within business entities, from the technology product or process innovation programs,
to broader perspective addressing innovation as a holistic strategic management
imperative not limited to research & development or New Product Development.
 The course takes you through Innovation related concepts, models, tools and
frameworks born out of Creative thinking, Various types of Innovations, Design
Thinking, Process of Innovation, Process of Innovation Management and Developing
Innovation Strategy.
 The course intends to build the competency among participants to be able to practice
Innovation at an individual level (development of new products & services) as well as
Managing Innovation at an organizational level to get a competitive advantage.

Objectives:

e With Innovation being an imperative for any organization to maintain its leadership in
the highly competitive environment, it is important for all Business owners and future
employees of the organizations to understand the all-important concepts & processes
related to Innovation.

e The course is essentially about building and sustaining innovation within organizations
by creating an innovative and learning organization. It aims to focus on innovation
within business entities, from the technology product or process innovation programs,
to broader perspective addressing innovation as a holistic strategic management
imperative not limited to research & development or New Product Development.

e The course takes you through Innovation related concepts, models, tools and
frameworks born out of Creative thinking, Various types of Innovations, Design
Thinking, Process of Innovation, Process of Innovation Management and Developing
Innovation Strategy.

e The course intends to build the competency among participants to be able to practice
Innovation at an individual level (development of new products & services) as well as
Managing Innovation at an organizational level to get a competitive advantage.

Outcomes:

After completion of the course, students would be able to:

e Participant will be able to use concepts, models and tools born out of Design thinking
to conceptualize new products & services

e Further they will learn how to assess market opportunity of Innovations and develop
Business plans to take them to market

e Participants will be able to understand how organizations use Innovation as their
business strategy

e Participants would be Equipped with the wherewithal of Managing the ‘Innovation
Funnel’ - Idea to Execution

seepage velocity and relation between them, factors affecting permeability of
soil, Determination of coefficient of permeability, Laboratory methods:

of stratified soils.

compaction specification and field control.

primary & secondary consolidation, Terzaghi’s spring analogy for
mechanism of consolidation, basic definitions, final settlement of soil
deposits, consolidation settlement: one-dimensional _ consolidation,
secondary consolidation.

Principal planes and principal stresses, Mohr-Coulomb theory, types of
shear tests, direct shear test, merits & demerits of direct shear test , tri-
axial compression tests, drainage conditions of UU, CU and CD tests,
unconfined compression test, vane shear test.

Introduction, methods of investigation, methods of boring, soil samplers
and sampling, number and disposition of borings, borehole logs.

Pre-requisite: Mechanics of Materials; Engineering Mechanics
Objectives:

2. To impart knowledge of analysis for determinate and indeterminate structures
3. To develop capability to calculate deflections of structures
4. To understand concept of plastic analysis
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Construct influence lines diagrams for determinate beams
2. Analyse indeterminate structure by Slope deflection and Moment Distribution Method
3. Evaluate deformations in various structures subjected to temperature change
4. Analyse indeterminate structure by flexibility and stiffness method
5. Plastic analysis of beams
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   General theorems: Theorems relating to elastic structures, principle of virtual   08
work. Strain energy in elastic structures, stresses due to axial load & impact
load. Complementary energy, Castigliano’s theorem, Betti’s and Maxwell’s
reciprocal theorems, principle of superposition. Types of structures occurring in
practice and their classification. Stable and unstable structure, static and
kinematic determinacy and indeterminacy of structure. Symmetric structure,
symmetrical and anti-symmetrical loads, distinction between linear and non-
linear behaviour of material and geometric non- linearity.
2   Deflection of statically determinate structures: Deflection of determinate pin   08
jointed and rigid jointed frames by principle of virtual work (unit load method)
and Castigliano’s theorem. Deflection due to temperature change.
3   Rolling loads and Influence lines for statically determinate structures:   08
Influence lines for cantilevers, simply supported, overhanging beams and pin
jointed truss, criteria for maximum shear force and bending moment at a
section, absolute maximum shear force and bending moment under moving loads
(udl and series of point loads) for simply supported beams.
4   Analysis of indeterminate structures by flexibility method: Flexibility   08
coefficients and their use in formulation of compatibility equations. Theorem of
three moments, Castigliano’s theorem of least work, application of above methods
to propped cantilevers, fixed beams, continuous beams excluding effect of
settlement of supports.
5   Analysis of indeterminate structures by stiffness method: Stiffness coefficients   09

capacity, Assumptions, Shape Factor for general sections. Collapse load and basic

condition.

Pre-requisite: Fundamental Knowledge of physics, chemistry and mathematics.
Objectives:
1. To provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living organisms from the
perspective of engineers.
2. To encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with
engineering tools.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are
diverse.
2. Identify DNA as a genetic material in the molecular basis of information transfer.
3. Classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action.
4. Apply thermodynamic principles to biological systems.
5. Identify and classify microorganisms.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Introduction: Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as
Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences
between science and engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and
camera, Bird flying and aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology
as an independent scientific discipline. Why we need to study biology?   03
Discuss how biological observations of 18th Century that lead to major
discoveries. Examples from Brownian motion and the origin of
thermodynamics by referring to the original observation of Robert Brown
and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight the fundamental
importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.
2.   Classification: Convey that classification per se is not what biology is all
about. The underlying criterion, such as morphological, biochemical or
ecological be highlighted. Hierarchy of life forms at phenomenological level.
A common thread weaves this hierarchy Classification. Discuss classification
based on (a) cellularity- Unicellular or multicellular (b) ultrastructure-
prokaryotes or eucaryotes. (c) energy and Carbon utilization -Autotrophs,   06
heterotrophs, lithotropes (d) Ammonia excretion – aminotelic, uricoteliec,
ureotelic (e) Habitata- acquatic or terrestrial (e) Molecular taxonomy- three
major kingdoms of life. A given organism can come under different category
based on classification. Model organisms for the study of biology come from
different groups. E.coli, S.cerevisiae, D. Melanogaster, C. elegance, A.
Thaliana, M. musculus
3.   Genetics: Convey that “Genetics is to biology what Newton’s laws are to   06
Physical Sciences” Mendel’s laws, Concept of segregation and independent
MBA TECH./CIVIL/2021-22/SEM-V/Page 15 of 19
SVKM's Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
assortment. Concept of allele. Gene mapping, Gene interaction, Epistasis.
Meiosis and Mitosis be taught as a part of genetics. Emphasis to be give not
to the mechanics of cell division nor the phases but how genetic material
passes from parent to offspring. Concepts of recessiveness and dominance.
Concept of mapping of phenotype to genes. Discuss about the single gene
disorders in humans. Discuss the concept of complementation using human
genetics.
4.   Biomolecules: Convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks
and yet the manifestations are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of
life. In this context discuss monomeric units and polymeric structures.   05
Discuss about sugars, starch and cellulose. Amino acids and proteins.
Nucleotides and DNA/RNA. Two carbon units and lipids.
5.   Enzymes: Convey that without catalysis life would not have existed on earth
Enzymology: How to monitor enzyme catalyzed reactions. How does an
enzyme catalyze reactions. Enzyme classification. Mechanism of enzyme   05
action. Discuss at least two examples. Enzyme kinetics and kinetic
parameters. Why should we know these parameters to understand biology?
RNA catalysis.
6.   Information Transfer: The molecular basis of coding and decoding genetic
information is universal Molecular basis of information transfer. DNA as a
genetic material. Hierarchy of DNA structure- from single stranded to   06
double helix to nucleosomes. Concept of genetic code. Universality and
degeneracy of genetic code. Define gene in terms of complementation and
recombination.
7.   Macromolecular analysis: How to analyses biological processes at the
reductionistic level Proteins- structure and function. Hierarch in protein   05
structure. Primary secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. Proteins as
enzymes, transporters, receptors and structural elements.
8.   Metabolism: The fundamental principles of energy transactions are the same
in physical and biological world. Thermodynamics as applied to biological
systems. Exothermic and endothermic versus endergonic and exergonic
reactions. Concept of Keq and its relation to standard free energy.   05
Spontaneity. ATP as an energy currency. This should include the breakdown
of glucose to CO2 + H2O (Glycolysis and Krebs cycle) and synthesis of
glucose from CO2 and H2O (Photosynthesis). Energy yielding and energy
consuming reactions. Concept of Energy Charge.
9.   Microbiology: Concept of single celled organisms. Concept of species and
strains. Identification and classification of microorganisms. Microscopy.
Ecological aspects of single celled organisms. Sterilization and media   04
compositions. Growth kinetics.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Theory of Structures
Objectives:
1. Analyse the indeterminate structures using advanced methods of analysis
2. Understand the concept of influence lines diagram for indeterminate beams
3. Understand the concept of approximate methods for analyse the portal frames
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Analyse the indeterminate structures using advanced methods of analysis
2. Plot the influence lines diagram for indeterminate beams
3. Analyse the portal frames using approximate methods
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Stiffness Method in Matrix Form:   13
Basic concepts of stiffness coefficients, member stiffness matrix for member of
plane truss, member of rigid jointed plane frame, member of plane grid and
member of space frame.
Properties of stiffness matrix, co-ordinate transformation matrix, stiffness matrix
in local and global co-ordinate axes system, assemblage of structural stiffness
matrix and application of boundary conditions.
Joint loads, Equivalent joint loads, method of solution for displacements and
computation of internal forces in members.
Application of stiffness method to beams, pin jointed trusses, rigid jointed
plane frames and simple plane grid structures.
2   Conventional Form of Stiffness Method, Modified Moment Distribution   07
Method:
Symmetric structure, Symmetric and anti-symmetric loads, Modification of
stiffness and carryover factors for symmetric and anti-symmetric loads both for
sway and non-sway cases for frames with different support conditions.
Application to frames involving side sways.
3   Flexibility Method in Matrix Form:   06
Review of concepts of flexibility coefficients, Selection of primary structure,
concept of structure flexibility matrix, compatibility equations, solution for
redundant forces, computational of internal forces, and joint displacements.
Application to pin jointed trusses and rigid jointed plane frames for different
loading including the effect of settlement of support, temperature changes and
elastic supports.
4   Conventional Form of Flexibility Method:   08
Elastic Center Method and its application to rectangular box, rigid jointed portal
frames and fixed arches.
Column Analogy Method and its application to analysis of non- prismatic beams,

simple rectangular frames, determination of stiffness coefficients and carry over
factors for non-prismatic beam members.

Muller Breslau’s Principle for drawing influence line diagrams for statically
indeterminate structures. Influence Lines Diagrams for propped cantilevers, fixed
beams and continuous beams.
6   Approximate Methods for Analysis of Building Frames:   05
Approximate methods for gravity loads: Substitute frame and equivalent
frames. Approximate methods for lateral loads: Portal and cantilever method.

Pre-requisite: Theory of structures, Concrete technology
Objectives:
1. To bring the students to such a level so as to enable them to take the appropriate decision in respect
of choice of prestressed section over R. C. C. as a civil engineer.
2. To make the candidate to understand the analysis of Prestressed Concrete sections and losses in
prestress.
3. To make the candidate able to understand and implement the guidelines of Indian Standard code
for analysis and design sections using limit state philosophy.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Understand the concept of pre-stressing its casting techniques and applications, behaviour of the
pre-stressed structures vis-à-vis that of the RCC structure.
2. Take the decision with respect to the choice of pre-stressed section over RCC.
3. Analyse the various pre-stressed components of the structure and design the same using relevant IS
Code.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction, Prestressing Systems and Material Properties:   07
Basic concept, early attempts of prestressing, brief history, development of building
materials. Definitions, advantages of prestressing, limitations of prestressing, types
of prestressing, source of prestressing force. External or internal prestressing, pre-
tensioning or post-tensioning, linear or circular prestressing, full, limited or partial
prestressing, uniaxial, biaxial or multiaxial prestressing. Prestressing systems and
devices. Constituents of concrete and hardened concrete, prestressing steel, codal
provisions.
2   Losses in Prestressed Concrete Section:   04
Notations, Losses in prestress, elastic shortening, pre-tensioned and post-tensioned
axial and flexural members. Friction loss, anchorage slip loss, force variation
diagram. Losses due to creep and shrinkage of concrete, relaxation of steel, total
time-dependent loss
3   Analysis of Members:   07
Analysis of members under axial load and flexure, analysis at service loads, stress
concept, force concept, load balancing concept. Cracking moment, kern point,
pressure line. Ultimate Strength, analysis of rectangular sections, flanged sections,
partially prestressed sections, un-bonded post-tensioned beams.
4   Design of Members:   07
Design of members for axial tension and flexure, design of prestressing force. Final
design, final design for Type – I and Type – II members. Choice of sections,
determination of limiting zone, post-tensioning in stages, Magnel’s graphical method,
detailing requirements for flexure, Shear and torsion.
5   Analysis and Design for Shear and Torsion:   07

Limit state of collapse for shear, maximum permissible shear stress, design of
transverse reinforcement, detailing requirement for shear, general comments, design
steps, design of stirrups for flange. Limit state of collapse for torsion, design of
longitudinal reinforcement, design of   transverse   reinforcement,   detailing
requirement for shear, general comments, design steps.
6   Calculations of Deflection and Crack Width:   02
Calculation of deflection, deflection due to gravity load, deflection due to
prestressing force, total deflection, limits of deflection, determination of moment of
inertia, limits of span-to-effective depth ratio, calculation of crack width, limits of
crack width.
7   Transmission of Prestress:   03
Introduction, Pre-tensioned members, transmission length, development length, end
zone reinforcement, post-tensioned members, end zone reinforcement, bearing
plate.
8   Continuous Beams:   04
Continuous Beams, introduction, analysis, incorporation of moment due to reactions,
pressure line due to prestressing force, concordant cable profile, cable profiles,
partially continuous beams, analysis at ultimate limit state, moment redistribution
9   Special Topics:   04
Circular prestressing, introduction, general analysis and design, prestressed concrete
pipes, liquid storage tanks, ring beams
Total   45

Objectives:

prototypes for a sustainable smart city
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to:

Pre-requisite: Introductory course in Environmental Studies, physics, chemistry, geography
Objectives:
1. Interpret multidisciplinary scientific bases of climatic change: basic mechanisms that govern the
climate system and its responses to drivers of change
2. Analyse paleo-climatic change and assess recent historical variability to project future climate
projections
3. Investigate the impact of climate change on communities of human population and global
economy
4. Gain insight into legal and Financial aspects of Climate change
5. Investigate fundamentals of the fields of Geo-engineering
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain how the climate system works and understand the physical basis of climate change
2. Investigate climate projections from the past and predict possible future climate change on Earth
3. Analyse how human activities are influencing Climate Change and Global Warming
4. Evaluate global climate change policy and its implementation, options for mitigation and
adaptation
5. Evaluate aspects of Climate change finance
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Climate Change Science:   08
 Human contribution to climate change; units of temperature, energy and
light;
 Overview of important greenhouse gases and their main sources, Earth
Energy Budget and Energy balance model, Radiative transfer, Naked planet
climate model, Nuclear winter
 Anthropogenic Drivers of Climate Change: Main observed changes in the
climate since the industrial revolution.
 Future trends and Impacts of Climate Change: Projected future trends and
impacts of climate change on surface temperature, precipitation, ocean pH
2   Paleo-Climate:   03
   Principles of Paleo-climate studies: Polar Regions and Sea level rise, Ice Ages
 Paleoclimate and Proxy Measurements
 Tree Rings, Borehole temperatures and Interglacial cycles
3   Climate and Changing Weather:   06
 Concepts of Heat transport, Coriolis Acceleration, Geostrophic motion, Ice
albedo, water vapour feedback, aerosols
 Global Wind Systems: Trade Winds and the Hadley Cell, the Highs and Lows
of the Westerlies, the Vital Importance of Monsoon Rains
 Cloud Formation and Climate: Hurricanes and Global Warming

 Global Ocean Circulation: The Icelandic Whirlpool, Origin of the Gulf
Stream, The Deep Atlantic Conveyor, El Niño and its Effects
 Global ice sheet degradation: rates, reasons
4   Climate Change Legalities:   06
 The Climate Change Policy Framework: Overview of how the international
legal and policy framework to address climate change developed over time
and key issues under negotiation.
 Key provisions of the UNFCCC, its organizational structure, and different
Party groups under the Convention.
 Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, COP Simulation
 Towards a Post-2020 Regime
 India’s role in climate change mitigation
6   Climate Change Adaptations and Finance:   08
 Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience: Conducting a Vulnerability
Assessment
 Climate Finance Landscapes
 Economic Development: Linking Adaptation and Development Planning;
international Initiatives to Support Climate Change Adaptation
   International Climate Negotiations
 Policy and Regulation
 National and International financing, Private Finance
 Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF), Green Climate Fund (GCF), WBG
2025 Climate Change, Pilot Program for Climate Resilience (PPCR)
7   Impacts of Climate Change: (Case Studies)   04
 On Ecosystems
 Food security and food production
 Human health, livelihoods and poverty
8   Geoengineering: Future technologies and Mitigation   10
 Overview of emissions levels and mitigation targets per country, ways to
integrate mitigation into development planning, through low emission
development strategies.
 Low Carbon Development, CO₂ Capture and Sequestration; role of basalt
rocks
 Solar Radiation Management, Temperature targets
   Biofuels, gas hydrates
 Slug Theory, stabilization scenarios
 Role of non-governmental organizations and corporate initiatives; voluntary
commitments and actions; disclosure-based initiatives; social cost of carbon
 Economics of Climate Change, main economic sectors where mitigation
actions can be applied
 Short term and Long Term Mitigation

Pre-requisite: Geology, Soil Mechanics, Foundation Engineering
Objectives:
1. To appreciate importance of geology in rock mechanics practice
2. To classify rocks based on various classification methods and predict their mechanical behavior
3. To understand laboratory and field techniques to determine stress –strain, modulus and strength
behaviour of rocks
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Appreciate importance of geology in rock mechanics practice
2. Classify rocks based on various classification methods and predict their mechanical behavior
3. Understand laboratory and field techniques to determine stress –strain, modulus and strength
behaviour of rocks
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Elements of structural geology:   03
Elements of Structural geology, geological site investigations in rocks and
engineering characteristics of rock masses, mapping of joints.
2   Engineering classification of rocks and rock masses:   08
Classification of intact rocks, rock mass classifications {rock quality designation,
rock   structural   rating, geomechanics   classification (RMR)}, strength and
modulus from classifications, classification based on strength and modulus,
Geoengineering, classification, Deere and Miller’s Engineering classification.
3   In-situ stress measurement in rocks and Rock testing:   09
a) In-situ stress measurement in rocks:
Flat Jack method, Bore-hole deformation method, Core discing method, Hydraulic
Fracturing method.
b) Rock testing:
1. Laboratory testing: Compression test, Effect of L/D ratio, Determination of
Modulus of Elasticity and Poisson's Ratio, Direct and Indirect (Brazilian) Tensile
tests, Shear tests (including hollow cylinder test).
2. 2. In-situ testing: Plate load test, Block shear test, Cable Jacking test,
Pressuremeter test.
4   Strength, modulus and stress-strain responses of rocks:   05
Factors influencing rock responses, strength criteria for isotropic intact rocks,
modulus of isotropic intact rocks with confining pressure, uni-axial compressive
strength of intact anisotropic rocks, strength due to induced anisotropy in rocks,
compressive strength and modulus from SPT, stress-strain models (constitutive
models, elastic stress-strain model, elasto-plastic stress-strain model, equivalent
material concept), influence of intermediate principal stress
MBA TECH./CIVIL/2021-22/SEM-VIII/Page 22 of 31
SVKM's Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
5   Bearing capacity of rocks:   10
Estimation of bearing capacity (foundation on intact rock, heavily fractured rock,
UBC with Hoek-Brown criterion, foundation on slope), stress distribution in rocks,
factor of safety, strengthening measures (concrete shear keys, bored concrete
piles, tensioned cable anchors, concrete block at toe), settlement in rocks (from joint
factor, for horizontal joints, from field tests)
6   Stability of rock slopes:   05
Modes of failure, rotational failure, plane failure, wedge method of analysis,
buckling failure, toppling failure, improvement of slope stability and protection
7   Rock bolting and grouting:   05
Opening in Rocks, Rock Bolting and Grouting Introduction to theory of
elasticity, lines and unlined tunnels, pressure tunnels and tunnels for other
purposes. Grouting in rocks, objectives, contact grouting, consolidation grouting,
process of grouting, grout requirement, types of grout, stage grouting, grout
curtain. Rock bolts, rock bolt types and applications, theory of rock bolting, rock
anchors, modes of failure, uplift capacity
Total   45

Course Rationale:

This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus and Linear

Algebra; It also aims to gradually develop in students an ability to apply these theoretical constructs to

solve problems within Engineering domain. This course covers Integration of single variable functions

and its applications, Differential calculus of single and multivariable functions, Matrix Algebra, Vector
Spaces, Linear Transformation and Eigen value problems.

Course Objectives:
1. To instill in prospective engineers knowledge of techniques in calculus, multivariate analysis and
linear algebra.

2. To equip the students with intermediate to advanced level concepts and aligned tools to help them
tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.

Course Outcomes:

After completion of the course, students would be able to:

1. employ the tool of beta, Gamma functions and evaluate integrals; apply the knowledge of integrals
to find surface areas and volumes of revolutions.

2. interpret mean value theorems and implement the concepts comprehensively; deploy power series
for advanced mathematical analysis.

3. operate and analyse functions of single and several variables and relate the results to real life
problems.

4, explain the key concepts of Vector Spaces and Linear Transformations such as Basis, Dimension,
Kernel and Range; and solve problems related to them.

5. solve Linear Systems of Equations, discuss Eigen Values and Vectors of Matrices and apply them
to solve engineering problems.

Pedagogy:
Lectures, tutorials, presentations, application-based videos, use of mathematical software.

Course Rationale:

This course aims to teach the fundamental concepts of Procedural Programming. Students will develop
skills related to problem solving by writing computer programs. This course does not require any prior
programming experience.

Course Objectives:

1. To enable students understand the basic concepts of Programming and help them build Programming
Logic.

2. To develop problem solving skills using basic Programming constructs, Decision Making and Looping.

3. To enable students solve complex problems using the knowledge of Arrays, Functions, Structures and
Pointers.

Course Outcomes:

After completion of the course, students would be able to :

1. formulate algorithms and draw flowcharts for arithmetic and logical problems
2. implement Decision Making, Nested Control Structures and Iterations

3. implement programs using Functions and concept of Recursion

4. demonstrate the use of Arrays, Strings, Structures and Pointers

5. apply Programming knowledge to solve searching and sorting problems

Course Rationale:
This course is intended to provide essential concepts in Chemistry. The contents have covered fundamentals of
chemistry required for students to apply the subject knowledge in engineering and technological applications.

Course Objectives:

1. To familiarize with atomic, molecular structure and chemical bonding of elements

2. To introduce electromagnetic spectrum ranges that are applied for various applications.

3. To acquaint with periodic properties of elements, thermodynamic parameters, cell emf and Nernst
equation.

4. To familiarize with stereochemistry and various organic reactions.

Course Outcomes:

After completion of the course, students would be able to :

1. understand basic concepts of atomic, molecular structure and chemical bonding of elements.

2, interpret various spectroscopic techniques like, electronic, vibrational-rotational and magnetic resonance.
3. rationalise periodic properties of the elements with electrochemistry.

4. solve numerical problems based on free energy & Nernst equation, EDTA as chelating agent.

5. recognize synthesis of organic molecules with respect to their structure and reactivity.

Experimental learning activities, presentations and lecture method.

Pre-requisite:
Knowledge of Senior Secondary Level English

Course Rationale :

The syllabus aims to develop a sound understanding of the basic concepts of English Language usage. Also,
the course prepares the students for developing their interpersonal communication, eventually leading to
enhanced employability skills.

Course Objectives:

1. To equip students with the knowledge of basic concepts of English language
2. To build learners’ vocabulary for effective speaking and writing

3. To inculcate and strengthen learners’ technical writing skills

4, To enhance the learners’ communication skills for employability through adequate exposure to
exercises in reading, writing, listening and speaking

Course Outcomes:

After completion of the course, students would be able to:

1. acquire basic proficiency in English including skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking

2. understand the basic rules governing English with a purpose to apply them effectively, with a
substantially increased vocabulary base

3. prepare for various professional challenges through effective practice of technical writing and business
presentations

4. identify, interpret and formulate appropriate communication strategies in response to different socio-
cultural and professional contexts as per the need of the industry

Pedagogy:
Classroom teaching, classroom exercises and discussion, written assignments, practice worksheets,
presentations and role play

Pre-requisite: Physics, Chemistry
Objectives:

1. To evaluate the structure of the Earth, its working and processes

2. To be able to qualify and quantify the rocks and minerals with specific relevance to civil
engineering projects

3. To use the geological information while embarking on site selection for any civil
engineering project

4. To evaluate sites using geological investigations

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain various geological phenomena

2. Categorize various types of minerals, rocks depending upon their suitability
3. Prepare a report on geological investigation of site for Civil Engineering Projects

Detailed Syllabus:
Unit | Description Duration
1. | General Geology: 12

Scope of Geology, Relationship between geology and civil engineering,
Brief history of the formation of the crust of the Earth, Internal constitution
of the Earth.

Physical Geology / Geomorphology:

Erosion and weathering; types, reasons, products.

Erosion by natural agents like Wind, Running Water, Glacier, Sea,
Subsurface Water, Organisms; Different erosional processes, erosional
landforms and depositional landforms.

Structural Geology:

Structural elements: Dip, Strike, Hade.

Folds: Classification schemes, superposed folding, causes of folding.
Faults: Nomenclature and classification schemes. Recognition in field and
effect on outcrops.

Joints: Types.

Unconformities: Types.

2. | Geotectonics: 06
Concept of plate tectonic theory, types of plate movements, mountain
building and sea floor spreading, Case studies like Himalayas, Atlantic
Ocean, New Zealand ete.

3. | Mineralogy: 04
Physical properties of minerals for identification, Concept of mineral
provinces: Case studies, Common primary and secondary minerals: Quartz

Pre-requisite: Physics
Objectives:

1. The objective of this Course is to provide an introductory treatment of Engineering
Mechanics to all the students of engineering, with a view to prepare a good foundation for
taking up advanced courses in the area in the subsequent semesters

2. A working knowledge of statics with emphasis on force equilibrium and free body diagrams
provides an understanding of the kinds of stress and deformation and how to determine
them in a wide range of simple, practical structural problems, and an understanding of the
mechanical behaviour of materials under various load conditions.

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:

1. Determine resultant forces and equilibrium of various force systems.

2. Determine centroid and moment of inertia of plane areas,

3. Determine the displacement, velocity, acceleration & their components for a moving

particle and rigid body.
4. Determine forces produced due to motion of particles and rigid body.
Detailed Syllabus;
Unit | Description Duration
I System of Forces: 8

Resultant of coplanar concurrent and non-concurrent forces, Resultant of
concurrent and non-concurrent forces in space

Equilibrium:

Equilibrium of system of concurrent and non-concurrent forces in plane
and space, Free body diagrams,

2. Application of Coplanar Forces and Equilibrium: 8
Trusses: Evaluation of member forces using method of sections and
method of joints.
Beams: Evaluation of reactions using equilibrium and principle of virtual
work
Simple frames: Evaluation of reactions using equilibrium

3. Friction: 5
Types of friction, Limiting friction, Laws of Friction, Static and Dynamic
Friction; wedge friction, screw jack

4. Centroid and Centre of Gravity: 6
Centroid of simple figures from first principle, centroid of composite
sections; Centre of Gravity and its implications; Area moment of inertia-
Definition, Moment of inertia of plane sections from first principles,
Moment of inertia of standard sections and composite sections; Mass
moment inertia of circular plate, Cylinder, Sphere

Pre-requisite: Fundamental Knowledge of physics, chemistry and mathematics.
Objectives:

1. To provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living organisms from the
perspective of engineers.
2. To encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with
engineering tools.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are
diverse.
2. Identify DNA asa genetic materia! in the molecular basis of information transfer.
3. Classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action.
4, Apply thermodynamic principles to biological systems.
5. Identify and classify microorganisms.

Detailed Syllabus:
Unit | Description Duration
I. Introduction 3

Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as Mathematics,
Physics and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences between
science and engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and camera,
Bird flying and aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an
independent scientific discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss
how biological observations of 18th Century that lead to major discoveries.
Examples from Brownian motion and the origin of thermodynamics by
referring to the original observation of Robert Brown and Julius Mayor.
These examples will highlight the fundamental importance of observations
in any scientific inquiry.

2. Classification
Convey that classification per se is not what biology is all about. The
underlying criterion, such as morphological, biochemical or ecological! be
highlighted. Hierarchy of life forms at phenomenological level. A common
thread weaves this hierarchy Classification. Discuss classification based on
(a) cellularity- Unicellular or multicellular (b) ultrastructure- prokaryotes
or eucaryotes. (c) energy and Carbon utilization -Autotrophs, heterotrophs, 6
lithotropes (4) Ammonia excretion — aminotelic, uricoteliec, ureotelic (e)
Habitata- acquatic or terrestrial (e) Molecular taxonomy- three major
kingdoms of life. A given organism can come under different category
based on classification. Model organisms for the study of biology come
from different groups. E.coli, S.cerevisiae, D. Melanogaster, C. elegance,
DS A. Thaliana, M. musculus.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering

3. Genetics

Convey that “Genetics is to biology what Newton’s laws are to Physical
Sciences” Mendel’s laws, Concept of segregation and independent
assortment. Concept of allele. Gene mapping, Gene interaction, Epistasis.
Meiosis and Mitosis be taught as a part of genetics. Emphasis to be give
not to the mechanics of cell division nor the phases but how genetic
material passes from parent to offspring. Concepts of recessiveness and
dominance. Concept of mapping of phenotype to genes. Discuss about the
single gene disorders in humans.

Discuss the concept of complementation using human genetics.

4, Biomolecules
Convey that all forms of life has the same building blocks and yet the
manifestations are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of life. In this
context discuss monomeric units and polymeric structures. Discuss about
sugars, starch and cellulose. Amino acids and proteins. Nucleotides and
DNA/RNA. Two carbon units and lipids.

5. Enzymes
Convey that without catalysis life would not have existed on earth
Enzymology: How to monitor enzyme catalyzed reactions. How does an
enzyme catalyze reactions. Enzyme classification. Mechanism of enzyme 5
action. Discuss at least two examples. Enzyme kinetics and kinetic
parameters, Why should we know these parameters to understand biology?
RNA catalysis.

6. Information Transfer
The molecular basis of coding and decoding genetic information is
universal Molecular basis of information transfer. DNA as a genetic
material. Hierarchy of DNA structure- from single stranded to double helix 6
to nucleosomes. Concept of genetic code. Universality and degeneracy of
genetic code. Define gene in terms of complementation and recombination.

7, Macromolecular analysis
How to analyses biological processes at the reductionistic tevel
Proteins- structure and function. Hierarch in protein structure. Primary
secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. Proteins as enzymes,
transporters, receptors and structural elements.

8. Metabolism

The fundamental principles of energy transactions are the same in physical

and biological world. Thermodynamics as applied to biological systems.
Exothermic and endothermic versus endergonic and exergonic reactions.
Concept of Keq and its relation to standard free energy. Spontancity. ATP 5
as an energy currency. This should include the breakdown of glucose to

CO2 + H20 (Glycolysis and Krebs cycle) and synthesis of glucose from

CO2 and H20 (Photosynthesis). Energy yielding and energy consuming
reactions. Concept of Energy Charge.

9. Microbiology
Concept of single celled organisms. Concept of species and strains.
Identification and classification of microorganisms. Microscopy. 4
Ecological aspects of single celled organisms. Sterilization and media
compositions. Growth kinetics.

Total 45

Objectives:

to various loads

2, Understand the mechanism to evaluate material properties

3. Understand the concept of principal stresses and their use

4, Understand the concepts of deflections of the members

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Evaluate internal forces and stresses produced in the deformable bodies

2. Analyse members subjected to flexure, shear and torsion
3, Evaluate deformations of determinate beams
4, Evaluate physical and mechanical properties of materials in laboratory

Unit | Description Duration

1 | Stress & strain: 09
Stress, yield stress, ultimate stress, shear stress, factor of safety, strain,
modulus of elasticity (E), modulus of rigidity (G), bulk modulus (K),
Poisson’s ratio, relationship between elastic constants, elongation due to
self-weight, bars of varying sections, stresses in composite section,
temperature stresses.

Axial force, shear force & bending moment diagrams for statically
determinate beams including beams with internal hinges for different
types of loading, relationship between rate of loading, shear force and
bending moment.

Flexure formula for beam, simple problems involving the application of
flexure formula, section modulus, moment of resistance of a section,
concepts of flitched/ composite beams. Distribution of shear stress across
plane sections used commonly for beams, shear connectors.

4 | Simple theory of torsion: 04
Torsion of circular shafts - solid and hollow, stresses and strains in shaft
when transmitting power.

Application to members subjected to eccentric loads and chimneys, core
of the section.

Pre-requisite: Mechanics of Materials; Engineering Mechanics
Objectives:
1. To introduced concept of influence lines
2. To impart knowledge of analysis for determinate and indeterminate structures
3. To develop capability to calculate deflections of structures
4. To understand concept of plastic analysis
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Construct influence lines diagrams for determinate beams
2. Analyse indeterminate structure by Slope deflection and Moment Distribution Method
3. Evaluate deformations in various structures subjected to temperature change
4. Analyse indeterminate structure by flexibility and stiffness method
5. Plastic analysis of beams
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   General theorems:   08
Theorems relating to elastic structures, principle of virtual work. Strain energy in
elastic structures, stresses due to axial load & impact load. Complementary
energy, Castigliano’s theorem, Betti’s and Maxwell’s reciprocal theorems,
principle of superposition
Types of structures occurring in practice and their classification. Stable and
unstable structure, static and kinematic determinacy and indeterminacy of
structure. Symmetric   structure, symmetrical and   anti-symmetrical   loads,
distinction between linear and non-linear behaviour of material and geometric
non- linearity.
2   Deflection of statically determinate structures:   08
Deflection of determinate pin jointed and rigid jointed frames by principle of
virtual work (unit load method) and Castigliano’s theorem. Deflection due to
temperature change.
3   Rolling loads and Influence lines for statically determinate structures:   08
Influence lines for cantilevers, simply supported, overhanging beams and pin
jointed truss, criteria for maximum shear force and bending moment at a
section, absolute maximum shear force and bending moment under moving loads
(udl and series of point loads) for simply supported beams.

4   Analysis of indeterminate structures by flexibility method:   08
Flexibility   coefficients   and their use in   formulation   of   compatibility
equations. Theorem of three moments, Castigliano’s theorem of least work,
application of above methods to propped cantilevers, fixed beams, continuous
beams excluding effect of settlement of supports.
5   Analysis of indeterminate structures by stiffness method:   09
Stiffness coefficients for prismatic members and their use for formulation of
equilibrium equations, direct stiffness method, slope deflection method, Moment
distribution method. Application of the above methods to indeterminate beams and
simple rigid jointed non-sway frames excluding the effect of settlement of
supports.
6   Plastic Analysis:   04
Introduction, Definitions of plastic hinge and plastic moment capacity,
Assumptions, Shape Factor for general sections. Collapse load and basic theorems
for finding collapse loads. Methods of plastic analysis – static method and
kinematic method, application of above method for beams.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Soil Mechanics
Objectives:
1. To get acquainted with effective and neutral stresses
2. To impart knowledge of lateral earth pressure theories
3. To get acquainted with bearing capacity of soils
4. To impart knowledge of analysis of axially loaded piles
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Analyze the soil – water characteristics and its effect on soil behaviour
2. Differentiate between active and passive conditions and apply Rankine and Coulomb’s
methods for different backfill situations
3. Estimate safe bearing capacity depending on site conditions.
Design single pile under axial load.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Effective and Neutral stresses   05
Introduction, effective stress principle, nature of effective stress, effect of water
table, effective stress in soils saturated by capillary action, seepage pressure,
critical hydraulic gradient, quick sand condition.
2   Lateral Earth Pressure Theories   10
Introduction, applications of earth pressure theories, different types of earth
pressures - at rest, active and passive pressures, Rankine’s earth pressure
theory, active earth pressure and passive earth pressure for horizontal and
inclined backfills, earth pressure for cohesionless and cohesive soils, Coulomb’s
wedge theory, Coulomb’s active and passive earth pressures in cohesionless
soils.
3   Bearing Capacity   09
Definitions of ultimate bearing capacity, gross, net and safe pressures,
allowable bearing pressure, types of shallow foundations, modes of failures,
bearing capacity theories by Terzaghi and Vesic, concept behind derivation of
Terzaghi’s general bearing capacity equation, bearing capacity equations for
rectangular, square and circular footings, factors influencing bearing capacity,
water table effect, performance of footings in different soils.

Pre-requisite: Fundamental Knowledge of physics, chemistry and mathematics.
Objectives:
1. To provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living organisms from the
perspective of engineers.
2. To encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with
engineering tools.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are
diverse.
2. Identify DNA as a genetic material in the molecular basis of information transfer.
3. Classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action.
4. Apply thermodynamic principles to biological systems.
5. Identify and classify microorganisms.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Introduction
Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as Mathematics,
Physics and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences between
science and engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and camera,
Bird flying and aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an
independent scientific discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss   03
how biological observations of 18th Century that lead to major discoveries.
Examples from Brownian motion and the origin of thermodynamics by
referring to the original observation of Robert Brown and Julius Mayor.
These examples will highlight the fundamental importance of observations in
any scientific inquiry.
2.   Classification
Convey that classification per se is not what biology is all about. The
underlying criterion, such as morphological, biochemical or ecological be
highlighted. Hierarchy of life forms at phenomenological level. A common
thread weaves this hierarchy Classification. Discuss classification based on   06
(a) cellularity- Unicellular or multicellular (b) ultrastructure- prokaryotes or
eucaryotes. (c) energy and Carbon utilization -Autotrophs, heterotrophs,
lithotropes (d) Ammonia excretion – aminotelic, uricoteliec, ureotelic (e)
Habitata- acquatic or terrestrial (e) Molecular taxonomy- three major

kingdoms of life. A given organism can come under different category based
on classification. Model organisms for the study of biology come from
different groups. E.coli, S.cerevisiae, D. Melanogaster, C. elegance, A.
Thaliana, M. musculus
3.   Genetics
Convey that “Genetics is to biology what Newton’s laws are to Physical
Sciences” Mendel’s laws, Concept of segregation and independent
assortment. Concept of allele. Gene mapping, Gene interaction, Epistasis.
Meiosis and Mitosis be taught as a part of genetics. Emphasis to be give not   06
to the mechanics of cell division nor the phases but how genetic material
passes from parent to offspring. Concepts of recessiveness and dominance.
Concept of mapping of phenotype to genes. Discuss about the single gene
disorders in humans.
Discuss the concept of complementation using human genetics.
4.   Biomolecules
Convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the
manifestations are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of life. In this   05
context discuss monomeric units and polymeric structures. Discuss about
sugars, starch and cellulose. Amino acids and proteins. Nucleotides and
DNA/RNA. Two carbon units and lipids.
5.   Enzymes
Convey that without catalysis life would not have existed on earth
Enzymology: How to monitor enzyme catalyzed reactions. How does an
enzyme catalyze reactions. Enzyme classification. Mechanism of enzyme   05
action. Discuss at least two examples. Enzyme kinetics and kinetic
parameters. Why should we know these parameters to understand biology?
RNA catalysis.
6.   Information Transfer
The molecular basis of coding and decoding genetic information is universal
Molecular basis of information transfer. DNA as a genetic material. Hierarchy   06
of DNA structure- from single stranded to double helix to nucleosomes.
Concept of genetic code. Universality and degeneracy of genetic code. Define
gene in terms of complementation and recombination.
7.   Macromolecular analysis
How to analyses biological processes at the reductionistic level
Proteins- structure and function. Hierarch in protein structure. Primary   05
secondary,   tertiary and quaternary   structure. Proteins as enzymes,
transporters, receptors and structural elements.
8.   Metabolism
The fundamental principles of energy transactions are the same in physical
and biological world. Thermodynamics as applied to biological systems.
Exothermic and endothermic versus endergonic and exergonic reactions.
Concept of Keq and its relation to standard free energy. Spontaneity. ATP as   05
an energy currency. This should include the breakdown of glucose to CO2 +
H2O (Glycolysis and Krebs cycle) and synthesis of glucose from CO2 and
H2O (Photosynthesis). Energy yielding and energy consuming reactions.
Concept of Energy Charge.

Pre-requisite: Theory of Structures
Objectives:
1. To make students familiar with behaviour of steel structure and their components under the action
of loads.

2. To train the students for effective use of IS codes, design tables and aids in analysing and designing
the steel structures by limit state method.

3. To equip students with aspects required for designing tension members, compression members and
column bases.

4. To equip students with aspects required for designing beams.

5. To help students design connections in steel members.

6. ‘lo aid students in designing steel trusses.

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain the Limit State Design philosophy as applied to steel structures

2. Demonstrate ability to follow IS codes, design tables and aids in analysis and design of steel
structures

3. Design columns and their bases
4. Design the various end connections for beams and trusses
5. Design steel trusses subjected to live load and wind load

Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)

Unit | Description Duration

1 Introduction to Steel structures: 02
Introduction to types of steel, mechanical properties of steel, advantages of steel as
structural material, design philosophies of Working Stress Method (WSM) and
Limit State Method (LSM)

2 Introduction to Limit State Method: 04
Limit state method, limit state of strength and serviceability (deflection, vibration,
durability, fatigue, fire), characteristics and design loads, Classification of cross
section- plastic, compact, semi-compact and slender, limiting width to thickness

ratio.

2 Axially loaded and Eccentrically loaded connections: 05
Introduction to bolted and welded axially and eccentrically loaded connections by
LSM.

4 Design of Tension members: 04

Design of tension members with welded / bolted end connections using single
and double angle sections by LSM, design strength due to- yiclding of gross
section, rupture of critical section and block shear.

Design of compression members with welded / bolted end connections using
single and double angle by LSM, design strength, effective length of compression
members.
Design of columns with single and built-up sections, design of lacing and batten
plates with bolted and welded connections using LSM, column buckling curves,

effective length, slenderness ratio, limiting values of effective slenderness ratio,
buckling class of various cross sections.

6 Design of Column bases: 06

Design of slab base and gusseted base using bolted and welded connection by
LSM subjected to axial load, Effective area of a base plate.

dL Design of Beams and Beam End Connections: 10
Design of members subjected to bending by LSM, design strength in bending,
effective length, laterally supported and unsupported beams, single and built-up
rolled steel sections using bolted and welded connections, shear lag effect, design
for shear, web buckling and web crippling, beam to beam and beam to column
connections, design of framed, un- stiffened and stiffened seat connections.

Total 45

Pre-requisite: Soil Mechanics; Foundation Engineering

Objectives:
1. To estimate stresses in soil
2. To analyse stability of earth slopes
3. To analyse earth retaining structures
4. To estimate bearing capacity of shallow and group of pile foundation

Outcomes:
After completion of this course, students would be able to:
1. Estimate stresses in soil using appropriate theories
2. Distinguish between types of slope failures, and analyze the stability of earth slopes
3. Analyse earth retaining structures like gravity and cantilever retaining walls
4. Analyse and estimate bearing capacity and settlement of shallow and pile foundations

Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)

Unit Description Duration

1 Stress distribution in soils: 06
Introduction, Boussinesq’s theory, vertical stress distribution diagrams,
construction of isobars, Pressure bulbs, Influence coefficients, vertical stresses
beneath loaded areas - point load, line load, uniformly loaded rectangular and
circular areas, Newmark’s influence chart, Westergaard’s analysis

2 Consolidation of soils: 06
Introduction to consolidation, basic definitions, spring analogy, computation of
total settlement, Terzaghi’s one-dimensional theory of consolidation, secondary
consolidation, degree of consolidation, time rate of consolidation, computation
of rate of settlements, determination of cv from consolidation test results, square
root of time and logarithm of time methods

3 Stress and strain behaviour of soils: 04
Shear strength of sands and clays, triaxial test - drained and undrained
behaviour of sands and clays, Skempton’s pore pressure Strain softening and
strain hardening, Octahedral plane, Mohr - Coulomb’s criterion, ideal, plastic,
and real soil behaviour

4, Stability of slopes: 06
Introduction, types of slope failure, different factors of safety, analysis of
infinite slopes, Stability of finite slopes- plane failure, Swedish circle method,
friction circle stability numbers and charts

Unit | Description Duration

1 |Substructure Construction: 10
Box jacking, pipe jacking, under water construction of diaphragm walls and
basement, tunnelling techniques, piling techniques, driving well and caisson,
sinking cofferdam, cable anchoring and grouting, driving diaphragm walls, sheet

1   Introduction to Stiffness Method in Matrix Form:   13
Basic concepts of stiffness coefficients, member stiffness matrix for member of
plane truss, member of rigid jointed plane frame, member of plane grid and
member of space frame.
Properties of stiffness matrix, co-ordinate transformation matrix, stiffness matrix
in local and global co-ordinate axes system, assemblage of structural stiffness
matrix and application of boundary conditions.

computation of internal forces in members.

plane frames and simple plane grid structures.

Symmetric structure, Symmetric and anti-symmetric loads, Modification of
stiffness and carryover factors for symmetric and anti-symmetric loads both for
sway and non-sway cases for frames with different support conditions.
Application to frames involving side sways.
3   Flexibility Method in Matrix Form:   06
Review of concepts of flexibility coefficients, Selection of primary structure,
concept of structure flexibility matrix, compatibility equations, solution for
redundant forces, computational of internal forces, and joint displacements.
Application to pin jointed trusses and rigid jointed plane frames for different
loading including the effect of settlement of support, temperature changes and
elastic supports.
4   Conventional Form of Flexibility Method:   08
Elastic Center Method and its application to rectangular box, rigid jointed portal
frames and fixed arches.
Column Analogy Method and its application to analysis of non- prismatic beams,

prestress.

for analysis and design sections using limit state philosophy.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:

Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction, Prestressing Systems and Material Properties:   07
Basic concept, early attempts of prestressing, brief history, development of building
materials. Definitions, advantages of prestressing, limitations of prestressing, types
of prestressing, source of prestressing force. External or internal prestressing, pre-
tensioning or post-tensioning, linear or circular prestressing, full, limited or partial
prestressing, uniaxial, biaxial or multiaxial prestressing. Prestressing systems and

time-dependent loss

concept, force concept, load balancing concept. Cracking moment, kern point,
pressure line. Ultimate Strength, analysis of rectangular sections, flanged sections,
partially prestressed sections, un-bonded post-tensioned beams.

design, final design for Type – I and Type – II members. Choice of sections,
determination of limiting zone, post-tensioning in stages, Magnel’s graphical method,
detailing requirements for flexure, Shear and torsion.

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Determine the dynamic properties of vibratory structures.
2. Determine the response of SDOF structure subjected to dynamic loads and base excitation
3. Determine the response of MDOF structure subjected to dynamic loads and base excitation
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction:   02
Introduction to structural dynamics, definition of basic problem in dynamics,
static v/s dynamic loads, different types of dynamic loads.
2   Single degree of Freedom (SDOF) systems:   18
Undamped vibration of SDOF system, natural frequency and period of vibration,
damping in structures, viscous damping and coulomb damping, effect of damping
on frequency of vibration and amplitude of vibration, logarithmic decrement.
Forced vibration, response to harmonic forces, periodic loading, dynamic load
factors, response of structure subjected to general dynamic load, Duhamel's
integral, numerical evaluation of dynamics response of SDOF systems subjected to
different types of dynamic loads. Introduction to frequency domain analysis,
response of structure in frequency domain subjected to general periodic and non-
periodic / impulsive forces of short duration, use of complex frequency response
function. Use of Fourier Series for periodic forces, introduction to vibration
isolation. Distributed mass system idealized as SDOF system, use of Rayleigh's
method, response of SDOF system subjected to ground motion.
3   Generalized Single-Degree of Freedom System:   06
Generalized properties, assemblages of rigid bodies, systems with distributed mass
and elasticity, expressions for generalized system properties.
4   Lumped mass multi degree of freedom (MDOF) system:   13
Coupled and uncoupled systems, direct determination of frequencies of
vibration and mode shapes, orthogonality principle, vibration of MDOF systems
with   initial conditions, approximate methods of determination of natural
frequencies of vibration and mode shapes-vector iteration methods, energy

loads.
5   Structure with distributed mass system:   06
Use of partial differential equation, free vibration analysis of single span beams
with various boundary conditions, determination of frequencies of vibration and
mode shapes, forced vibration of single span beams subjected to the action of

2. calculate the external stability and internal stability of backfilled walls
3. Study the stability parameters related to soil reinforcement and anchoring
4. Design sheet pile walls
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Earth pressure:   08
Introduction, classification of retaining walls in terms of structural functionality,
Lateral Earth Pressure at Rest, Rankine’s and coulomb’s active earth state,
Rankine’s and coulomb’s passive earth state, Culmann’s graphical solution,
earthquake effect on active and passive states: Mononobe Okabe equations,
numerical problems.
2   Introduction to design and backfilled walls:   02
Limit States for earth retaining structures, factors to consider in choosing a retaining
structure, types of structures, selection and acquisition of soil parameter, types of
analysis.

calculations, overturning, sliding, bearing capacity, overall stability, settlement and
tilt, numerical problems.
Internal Stability - masonry, gravity block and gabion walls, crib walls, reinforced
concrete cantilever walls. Design Problems.
4   Soil reinforcement and anchoring:   12
Mechanics of Reinforced soil - enhancement of shear strength, available
reinforcement force, stress-strain behaviour.
Components of reinforced soil walls - reinforcement, facing, backfill.
Principles of Design - general, preliminary dimensions, factors of safety, provisions
of FHWA NHI-0043 (2001)
External Stability - outward sliding, overturning.
Internal Stability - tension failure, pull-out failure.
Pull-out capacity of reinforcement - strip reinforcement, bar reinforcement (soil
nails), sheet/fabric reinforcement, wire mesh reinforcement, polymer grid
reinforcement, bar anchor reinforcement, hybrid anchoring systems, numerical
problems.
Ground Anchors - types of ground anchor, design of ground anchor, durability.

Cantilever sheet-pile walls - preliminary design, determination of depth of

that underpins it. The course is designed to help the students develop innovative concepts and
prototypes for a sustainable smart city
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Decode the Smart City concept & different models of Smart cities in the world
2. Application of technological innovations for smart city enablement
3. Identify and measure requirements of a smart city.
4. Project work: Generate innovative solutions for smart city as projects outcome
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1. “Smart City” – Various perspectives and definitions, Characteristics of a   3
smart city
What makes a city Smart? What are the different models of Smart city
development – existing city into Smart city, New green field project,
enhancing a “town” into a Smart City.
2. Components of a smart city   3
Pillars of a smart city – Institutional, Physical, Social, Economic,
Infrastructure, Factors that make smart cities possible, Use of technology and
automation.
3.   Identification of smart cities: Framework and KPI for smart city   3
development - 1
Conditions precedent for smart city development, Benchmarks for smart cities,
Government   policies, Mapping of smart   cities through   Transport,
Infrastructure, Water Management, energy, health, hygiene & sanitation,
education, governance, social & cultural fabric and disaster management.
Measurement of key parameters (KPI) for smart cities

4. Technological framework of smart cities.   3

Sensing, data aggregation, analytic/optimization and visualization
technologies
6. Understanding Financial sustainability of Smart cities, the PPP model   3
for smart city development
7. Case Studies of Existing best practices in cities in India   3
8. Case Studies of Existing Smart cities of the world   3
Like Singapore, London – UK, Barcelona etc.
9. Project work begins : Students get divided into teams, each team will   3
study one of the ten aspects of Smart city- Transport, Infrastructure,
Water Management , energy, health, hygiene & sanitation, education,
governance, social & cultural fabric and disaster management
Project work begins - Briefing to students on the sub-themes and allotted
projects related to any one area for an in- depth study by each team. The
stage gates and timelines for the project defined along with the evaluation
criteria at each deliverable.
10. Sector analysis - Project wise   3
Presentation of secondary research on the specific area picked up by the student
teams
11. Primary Research work - Project wise   3
Expert interviews, focus group discussions, ethnographic study to understand
the needs and aspirations of people from the future cities.
12. Ideation for Innovative concept proposals for resolving issues in Smart   3
cities
Observation on post-it notes, Clustering, Analysis and ideation for new concept
ideas

Students develop concepts around proposed solutions for various pain points
identified in their respective domain areas
14. Feasibility Analysis of the Concepts developed   3
Concepts developed initially put through feasibility tests and refined
subsequently

generated

Pre-requisite: Introductory course in Environmental Studies, physics, chemistry, geography
Objectives:
1. Interpret multidisciplinary scientific bases of climatic change: basic mechanisms that govern the
climate system and its responses to drivers of change
2. Analyse paleo-climatic change and assess recent historical variability to project future climate
projections
3. Investigate the impact of climate change on communities of human population and global
economy
4. Gain insight into legal and Financial aspects of Climate change
5. Investigate fundamentals of the fields of Geo-engineering
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain how the climate system works and understand the physical basis of climate change
2. Investigate climate projections from the past and predict possible future climate change on Earth
3. Analyse how human activities are influencing Climate Change and Global Warming
4. Evaluate global climate change policy and its implementation, options for mitigation and
adaptation
5. Evaluate aspects of Climate change finance
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Climate Change Science:   08
 Human contribution to climate change; units of temperature, energy and
light;
 Overview of important greenhouse gases and their main sources, Earth
Energy Budget and Energy balance model, Radiative transfer, Naked planet
climate model, Nuclear winter
 Anthropogenic Drivers of Climate Change: Main observed changes in the
climate since the industrial revolution.
 Future trends and Impacts of Climate Change: Projected future trends and
impacts of climate change on surface temperature, precipitation, ocean pH
2   Paleo-Climate:   03
   Principles of Paleo-climate studies: Polar Regions and Sea level rise, Ice Ages
 Paleoclimate and Proxy Measurements
 Tree Rings, Borehole temperatures and Interglacial cycles
3   Climate and Changing Weather:   06
 Concepts of Heat transport, Coriolis Acceleration, Geostrophic motion, Ice
albedo, water vapour feedback, aerosols
 Global Wind Systems: Trade Winds and the Hadley Cell, the Highs and Lows
of the Westerlies, the Vital Importance of Monsoon Rains
 Cloud Formation and Climate: Hurricanes and Global Warming

 Global Ocean Circulation: The Icelandic Whirlpool, Origin of the Gulf
Stream, The Deep Atlantic Conveyor, El Niño and its Effects
 Global ice sheet degradation: rates, reasons
4   Climate Change Legalities:   06
 The Climate Change Policy Framework: Overview of how the international
legal and policy framework to address climate change developed over time
and key issues under negotiation.
 Key provisions of the UNFCCC, its organizational structure, and different
Party groups under the Convention.
 Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, COP Simulation
 Towards a Post-2020 Regime
 India’s role in climate change mitigation
6   Climate Change Adaptations and Finance:   08
 Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience: Conducting a Vulnerability
Assessment
 Climate Finance Landscapes
 Economic Development: Linking Adaptation and Development Planning;
international Initiatives to Support Climate Change Adaptation
   International Climate Negotiations
 Policy and Regulation
 National and International financing, Private Finance
 Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF), Green Climate Fund (GCF), WBG
2025 Climate Change, Pilot Program for Climate Resilience (PPCR)
7   Impacts of Climate Change: (Case Studies)   04
 On Ecosystems
 Food security and food production
 Human health, livelihoods and poverty
8   Geoengineering: Future technologies and Mitigation   10
 Overview of emissions levels and mitigation targets per country, ways to
integrate mitigation into development planning, through low emission
development strategies.
 Low Carbon Development, CO₂ Capture and Sequestration; role of basalt
rocks
 Solar Radiation Management, Temperature targets
   Biofuels, gas hydrates
 Slug Theory, stabilization scenarios
 Role of non-governmental organizations and corporate initiatives; voluntary
commitments and actions; disclosure-based initiatives; social cost of carbon
 Economics of Climate Change, main economic sectors where mitigation
actions can be applied
 Short term and Long Term Mitigation

Pre-requisite: Geology, Soil Mechanics, Foundation Engineering
Objectives:
