Objectives:

1. To provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living organisms
from the perspective of engineers.

2. To encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems
with engineering tools.

Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the
manifestations are diverse.
2. Identify DNA as a genetic material in the molecular basis of information transfer.
3. Classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme
action.
4. Apply thermodynamic principles to biological systems.
5. Identify and classify microorganisms.

nor the phases but how genetic material passes from parent to
offspring. Concepts of recessiveness and dominance. Concept of
mapping of phenotype to genes. Discuss about the single gene
disorders in humans.

Discuss the concept of complementation using human genetics.

and formulate operations strategy in organizations.

Time (JIT), Six Sigma, Lean Production and Quality Function Deployment and their
applications and understand of Theory of Constraints.

Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This

including limits, derivatives, Mean Value Theorems, Taylor and Maclaurin series, and
LHospital’s rule. (K2)

series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s
method of undetermined multipliers. (K3)

4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and
coordinate transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes. (K3)
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year
students’ learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with
the required practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically,
solve challenging problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication
skills, teamwork and planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will
help broaden their scope and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms
and verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to
submit a report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional
simulation and synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before
examiners.

 Explain various operations management concepts

Course Outcomes

applications, and understand the Theory of Constraints..

Objectives:
 To sensitize students about criticality of operations function in a business organization.
 To impart students with the knowledge on various operations management issues and equip
them with skills to analyze them with effective corrective action and implementation.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Use basic operations function, operations management and productivity related to operations
and formulate operations strategy in organizations.
2. Recognize the processes, their types, layouts, process analysis and their applications and
undertake a detailed study on selection of suitable locations for manufacturing plants,
facilities and service centers.
3. Understand different production system with their advantages and disadvantages along with
a learning on Product-Process Matrix and job sequencing and scheduling methods.
4. Undertake a detailed study and learning of Inventory management systems and different
inventory control models with their applications.
5. Implement Quality Management, TQM concepts in an organization and appreciate Just in
Time (JIT), Six Sigma, Lean Production and Quality Function Deployment and their
applications and understand of Theory of Constraints.

Prerequisite:
 Contemporary Practices in Management
Objectives:
 With Innovation being an imperative for any organization to maintain its leadership in
the highly competitive environment, it is important for all Business owners and future
employees of the organizations to understand the all-important concepts & processes
related to Innovation.
 The course is essentially about building and sustaining innovation within organizations
by creating an innovative and learning organization. It aims to focus on innovation
within business entities, from the technology product or process innovation programs,
to broader perspective addressing innovation as a holistic strategic management
imperative not limited to research & development or New Product Development.
 The course takes you through Innovation related concepts, models, tools and
frameworks born out of Creative thinking, Various types of Innovations, Design
Thinking, Process of Innovation, Process of Innovation Management and Developing
Innovation Strategy.
 The course intends to build the competency among participants to be able to practice
Innovation at an individual level (development of new products & services) as well as
Managing Innovation at an organizational level to get a competitive advantage.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Participant will be able to use concepts, models and tools born out of Design thinking
to conceptualize new products & services
2. Further they will learn how to assess market opportunity of Innovations and develop
Business plans to take them to market
3. Participants will be able to understand how organizations use Innovation as their
business strategy

Course Objectives
The main objective of this course is to equip the students with the ability to solve, assemble and test
simple AC and DC electrical circuits. Further, the course also enables the student to obtain a basic
understanding of the working principle and applications of electronics devices.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. interpret DC circuits, theorems and time domain analysis of first order RL circuit,
2. solve series and parallel AC circuits and compare star/delta configurations,
3. explain the principles of transformer and electrical machines,
4. understand the construction, working principle and applications of electronics devices and
logic circuits
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1. DC Circuits   6
Electrical circuit elements (R, L and C), voltage and current sources, Kirchhoff’s
current law, Kirchhoff’s voltage laws, Analysis of simple circuits with dc
excitation, Superposition Theorem, Thevenin’s Theorems, Norton’s Theorems.
Time-domain analysis of first-order RL circuits.
2.   AC Circuits   8
Generation of alternating emf, instantaneous, rms, peak, average values and
related other terms, vector representation of AC quantities, Steady state analysis
of R, L, C series and parallel circuits, resonance. Generation of three-phase emf,

Course Objectives
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and its
principles. The students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of its
institutions vis a vis their relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to
1. Understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and to
understand the principles mentioned in its Preamble,
2. Inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions upon it so
as to enjoy these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously performing their
duties and to apply these principles into their professional lives,
3. Ingrain the structure of our polity and role of Judiciary in maintaining the basic structure of
the Constitution,
4. Attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know the
additional powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to
understand the Amendment procedure.

and 26, Right to remedy under Article 32 and Fundamental duties

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics , Partial Differential Equations and Laplace transforms
Course Objective
The course is aimed at delivering detailed understanding of fluid properties and their static - dynamic
nature. This course teaches the analytical techniques necessary for grasping fundamental behavior of
incompressible fluids. It is designed for the students to learn the principles of laminar flow, turbulent
flow, and boundary layer theory to solve important practical problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Differentiate fluid properties and their static- dynamic nature
2. Analyze fundamental behavior of incompressible fluid
3. Evaluate the fundamental behaviour of laminar and turbulent flow and boundary layer
theory to solve real life problems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1. Fluid Properties   03
Concept of continuum, fluid properties, Classification of fluid, Newton’s law
of viscosity, stress-strain relationship.
2. Fluid Statics   10
Basic hydrostatic equation, Pascal’s Law, application to Manometers and
mechanical gauges, hydrostatic forces on plane and curved submerged
surfaces.
Buoyancy and Floatation
Archimedes’ Principle, buoyancy force and centre of buoyancy, metacentre,
metacentric height, analytical method to find metacentric height, condition of
equilibrium of submerged bodies, oscillation of a floating body
3. Fluid Kinematics   08
Description of fluid motion-Lagrangian method and Euler’s method,
classification of flow types- steady and unsteady, uniform and non-uniform,
laminar and turbulent, one two and three- dimensional flow, rotational and
irrotational, laminar and turbulent, compressible and incompressible.
Flow patterns- stream lines, path lines, stream tubes and streak lines.
Continuity equation (Cartesian and polar co-ordinates), circulation and
vorticity, velocity potential and stream function.
MBA(Tech)/Mechanical/Sem-III/2022-23/Page 12
SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
4. Fluid Dynamics   09
Euler’s equation of motion, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications-venturimeter,
orificemeter, rotameter, pitot tube, Impulse-Momentum equation and   its
applications, Reynolds Transport Theorem and its application.
Dimensional Analysis
Secondary or derived quantities, Reyleigh method, Buckingham−𝜋theorem,
dimensionless numbers, Theory of similarity, Model laws.
5. Laminar Flow   10
Navier-Stokes equation of motion, developing expression for flow rate, pressure
drop, shear stress, friction factor. Flow of viscous fluid in circular pipes- Hagen
Poiseuille law, Couette flow.
Turbulent Flow
Shear stresses in turbulent flow, theories of turbulent shear stress, hydro-
dynamically smooth and rough surface, modeling of turbulence, Moody’s chart.
Flow Through Pipes
Energy losses in pipes: Minor and Major losses, Darcy-Weisbatch equation for head
loss in pipes, hydraulic gradient lines, and total energy lines, pipes in series and
parallel, Equivalent pipe.
6. Boundary Layer Theory   05
Concept of Boundary layer, Boundary layer over flat plate, Boundary Layer
thickness, momentum thickness, displacement thickness and energy thickness.
Boundary layer equations and their solutions. Blasius solution (without derivation),
Von-Karman momentum integral equation. Laminar boundary layer and turbulent
boundary layer. Separation and control and Concept of drag.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
This course focusses on the application of classical mechanics to various biological problems by
combining the fields of biology and physiology. This course is concerned with the application of
principles of mechanics to the conceptualization, design, development and analysis of equipment
and systems as applied to human body.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Correlate mechanics, biomechanics and kinesiology and differentiate between their uses in the
analysis of human movement
2. Relate the reference positions, planes, and axes associated with the human body
3. Evaluate the skeletal considerations for movement and the different mechanics involved in
bones
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Basic Terminology   05
Biomechanics, kinesiology, anatomy, functional anatomy
linear motion, angular motion, kinematics, kinetics, statics and dynamics.
2.   Kinematic Concepts for Analyzing Human Motion   05
Linear, angular and general motion, anatomical reference position, planes
and axes, joint movement terminology, spatial reference systems, analyzing
human movement and tools for measuring kinematic quantities.
3.   Applications of Statics to Biomechanics   10
Skeletal joints, skeletal muscles, mechanics of the elbow, mechanics of the
shoulder, mechanics of the spinal column, mechanics of the hip, mechanics
of the knee and mechanics of the ankle.
4.   Skeletal Considerations for Movement   10
Bone tissue function, composition of bone tissue, macroscopic structure of
bone, bone formation, strength and stiffness of bone, loads applied to bone,
stress fractures, articular cartilage, fibrocartilage and ligaments.

Course Objective
The objective of the course is to impart introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. The course is structured to
acquaint the students with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of additive manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application

Unit   Description   Duration

Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.

Process mechanism, process parameters, extrusion of: ceramics, metals,
biomaterials, composites, contour crafting, concrete printing

Rapid Liquid Printing.

Binder jettng process workflow, material requirements, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
Material Jetting process workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ.
Powder bed fusion AM process:

(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters
Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Processes:
Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net

Product quality evaluation, need for post-processing, support material
removal, surface finish improvement, aesthetic improvement, property
enhancements using non-thermal and thermal techniques.

Design guidelines: part orientation, support, geometry considerations, layer

Course Objective
This course focusses on a critical understanding and strategic importance of operations management.
The students can get familiar with interactions between firms based on parameters such as
information sharing, contracting and coordination in supply chain management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -

sector as well as manufacturing firms

procurement

order to generate greater benefit

of manufacturing processes. Plant location and types of plant layout.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Thermodynamics, Fluid Mechanics, Differential and Integral Calculus
Course Objective
This course is designed to provide knowledge of different modes of heat transfer with different laws
of conduction, convection and radiation. It also helps to provide understanding of different
applications of conduction, convection and radiation.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the basic laws of heat transfer
2. Analyse realistic problems involving different modes of heat transfer
3. Apply basic principles of heat transfer to design heat transfer devices
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Basic Concepts   15
Modes of Heat Transfer, its mechanism and mathematical models.
Conduction Heat Transfer
Fourier’s general conduction equation in Cartesian, Cylindrical and Spherical co-
ordinates (for cylindrical and spherical walls derivation of Fourier’s three-
dimensional equation is not included), thermal resistance, solution of Fourier’s
equation for one dimensional steady state heat conduction through various
configurations such as plane, cylindrical, spherical wall, composite medium.
Critical thickness of insulation and its importance.
Heat Transfer from Extended Surfaces
Types of fins, Governing equation, fin effectiveness, efficiency of fins, concept of
corrected fin length, application of fins.
Unsteady State Heat Conduction
Lumped System Analysis
2.   Convection Heat Transfer   15
Forced and natural convection, hydrodynamic and thermal boundary layer,
Convection heat transfer coefficient, Momentum and energy equation for laminar
boundary layer, Laminar and Turbulent flow, principles of dimensional analysis,
physical significance of dimensionless numbers, Nusselt number, Prandtl
number, Reynolds number, Grashof number.
Empirical relations and their use for forced internal and external convection for
circular and non-circular ducts.
Empirical relations and their use for free convection on vertical, horizontal flat
plate and cylinders.
Boiling and Condensation
Physical phenomenon and Pool boiling curve.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
3.   Thermal Radiation   07
Introduction to physical mechanism, concept of black body, grey body and
radiation properties. Microwave Heating.
Basic laws of radiation; Planck’s law, Kirchoff’s law, Stefan-Boltzman law,
Wein’s-displacement law and Lambert’s Cosine law, Intensity of radiation,
radiosity, shape factor for simple geometries, heat exchange between non-black
bodies, Radiation Shield.
4.   Heat Exchangers   08
Classification, temperature distribution in parallel and counter flow
arrangement, overall heat transfer coefficient, fouling factor, log mean
temperature difference method, Effectiveness-NTU method.
Total   45

Course Objective
This course provides the understanding of the development and design aspects of products, impart
knowledge of business and technical concerns about the different methodologies of product
development. This course also discusses the concept of product life cycle and product data
management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1.   Identify the different stages of product development and design with modern approaches
2. Apply the knowledge of Technology Forecasting using S-Curve in product development as
per customers need
3. Describe the process of benchmarking of products, technologies & techniques product design

Unit   Description   Duration

of design and redesign, design by evolution and innovation, factors in product

various phases, modern approaches- concurrent design in product development,
product development team and product development planning with reference to

Characteristics

regulations related to UAVs and various types of components, sensors, data processing, and hands-

To provide an understanding of the basics of aerodynamics in aircraft. To impart knowledge of
boundary layer theory. To introduce the aerospace vehicle and space vehicle design. To introduce
wind tunnel testing

After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Analyse the basic flight mathematical aspects and potential flows

Importance of Aerodynamic, four principles of aerodynamics, three laws of
aerodynamics, six fundamentals of flight.

body theories. Flight vehicle aerodynamics, rotor aerodynamics – low Reynolds
number aerodynamics

This course is designed to impart knowledge of an IC engine and the ignition systems. It also
introduces the modern developments in internal combustion engines with optical measurement
techniques and emission control.

After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain advanced engine technologies and emission norms

of internal combustion engines

Unit   Description   Duration

relative merits.

Course Objective
This course introduces the basic concepts of vibrations and discusses free vibration of an undamped
single-degree of-freedom system. This course also deals with two-degree-of-freedom systems, which
require two independent coordinates to describe their motion. The modeling of continuous
systems as multidegree-of-freedom systems is also presented in this course.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Derive the equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom system
2. Solve two-degree-of-freedom free- and forced-vibration problems
3. Formulate the equations of motion of multidegree-of-freedom systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Vibration   07
Basic Concepts of Vibration, Classification of Vibration, Vibration Analysis
Procedure, Spring Elements, Mass or Inertia Elements, Damping Elements,
Harmonic Motion, Harmonic Analysis
2.   Single-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   08
Free Vibration of an Undamped Translational System, Free Vibration of an
Undamped Torsional System, Free Vibration with Viscous Damping, Free
Vibration with Coulomb Damping.
3.   Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   06
Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration, Free Vibration Analysis of an
Undamped System, Torsional System, Forced-Vibration Analysis.
4.   Multidegree-of-Freedom Systems   09
Modeling of Continuous Systems as Multi degree of Freedom Systems, Equations
of Motion, Influence Coefficients, Generalized Coordinates and Generalized
Forces, Lagrange s Equations, Equations of Motion of Undamped Systems in
Matrix Form, Eigenvalue Problem

Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to the finite element methods. The guidelines for selecting
displacement functions and the concepts that should be considered when modeling are discussed as
the course progresses. This course describes how to treat different types of forces for two-dimensional
elements and to solve one-dimensional heat transfer problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Derive the stiffness matrix for the beam and Constant-Strain Triangular element
2. Describe some of the approximations essential in finite element solutions
3. Solve a heat transfer problem by the finite element method
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   07
Brief history, matrix notation, general steps, applications and advantages of the
FEM, computer programs for the FEM, stiffness matrix for a spring element,
spring assemblage, direct stiffness method, boundary conditions.
2.   Truss   08
Stiffness matrix for a bar element, displacement function, transformation of
vectors in two dimensions, global stiffness matrix for bar arbitrarily oriented in
the plane, computation of stress for a bar in the x – y plane, solution of a plane
truss, use of symmetry in structures, inclined supports.
3.   Beam and Frame   10
Beam stiffness, assemblage of beam stiffness matrices, direct stiffness method,
distributed loading, beam element with nodal hinge, two-dimensional arbitrarily
oriented beam element, rigid plane frame, skewed supports, beam element
arbitrarily oriented in space, concept of substructure analysis
4.   Plane Stress and Plane Strain   07
Concepts of Plane Stress and Plane Strain, Constant-Strain Triangular Element
Stiffness Matrix, Body and Surface Forces, Plane Stress Problem, Bilinear
Rectangle, Comparison of Elements

Pre-requisite: Physics
Objectives
The course is aimed at developing thorough understanding of physical and mathematical
principles used in mechanics. This course will help students get acquainted with the various
systems of forces and the importance of center of gravity. It is designed for the students to
master the concept of static equilibrium and its applications along with the development of
equations of motion for rigid bodies. The topics covered are tailored to suit the requirements
of an intermediate undergraduate level in engineering.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to
1. Determine the resultant / equilibrant of various systems of forces,
2. Analyse the system of forces in equilibrium,
3. Determine the centroid and moment of inertia of a plane area,
4. Evaluate the velocity, acceleration and displacement of a moving body along with
forces developed on rigid bodies subjected to displacements and rotations.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   System of forces:   12
Rectangular components of forces in space, moment of a force about a
point, moment of a force about a given axis, resultant of general force
system, Coplanar and non-coplanar force system, forces and their
components, resultant of coplanar force system - concurrent forces,
parallel forces, non-concurrent non-parallel system of forces, moment of
force about a point, couple, Varignon’s theorem. Concept of virtual work,
Principle of virtual work.
2   Application of system of forces and equilibrium   08
Free body diagram with examples on modelling of typical supports and
joints, condition for equilibrium in three and two dimensions.
Friction: Limiting and non-limiting cases, Laws of friction, angle of
friction, angle of repose, cone of friction, Equilibrium of bodies on rough
horizontal and inclined plane, application to problems involving wedges,
ladder. Belt friction, flat belts on the flat pulleys.

Centroid, moment of inertia, polar moment of inertia, and product of
inertia, parallel and perpendicular axis theorem.

Velocity and acceleration in terms of rectangular coordinate system,
rectilinear motion, motion along plane curved path, tangential and normal
component of acceleration, acceleration - time, velocity- time graphs and
their uses, relative velocity, projectile motion, simple harmonic motion.
Kinematics of rigid bodies:
Translation, pure rotation and plane motion of rigid bodies, instantaneous
centre of rotation for the velocity for bodies in plane motion, link
mechanisms (up to two links).

Newton’s laws of motion, D’Alembert’s principle, equation of dynamic
equilibrium, linear motion, curvilinear motion.

D’Alembert’s principle for bodies under translational motion, rotational

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics , Partial Differential Equations and Laplace transforms
Objectives
The course is aimed at delivering detailed understanding of fluid properties and their static-
dynamic nature. This course teaches the analytical techniques necessary for grasping
fundamental behavior of incompressible fluids. It is designed for the students to learn the
principles of laminar flow, turbulent flow, and boundary layer theory to solve important
practical problems.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to
1. Understand fluid properties and their static- dynamic nature,
2. Analyze fundamental behavior of incompressible fluid,
3. Understand and evaluate the fundamental behaviour of laminar and turbulent flow and
boundary layer theory to solve real life problems.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Fluid Properties: Concept of continuum, fluid properties, Classification of   03
fluid, Newton’s law of viscosity, stress-strain relationship.
2   Fluid Statics: Basic hydrostatic equation, Pascal’s Law, application to   10
Manometers and mechanical gauges, hydrostatic forces on plane and curved
submerged surfaces.
Buoyancy and Floatation: Archimedes’ Principle, buoyancy force and centre
of buoyancy, metacentre, metacentric height, analytical method to find
metacentric height, condition of equilibrium of submerged bodies, oscillation
of a floating body
3   Fluid Kinematics: Description of fluid motion-Lagrangian method and   08
Euler’s method, classification of flow types- steady and unsteady, uniform
and non-uniform, laminar and turbulent, one two and three- dimensional
flow, rotational and irrotational, laminar and turbulent, compressible and
incompressible.
Flow patterns- stream lines, path lines, stream tubes and streak lines.
Continuity equation (Cartesian and polar co-ordinates), circulation and
vorticity, velocity potential and stream function.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
4   Fluid Dynamics: Euler’s equation of motion, Bernoulli’s equation and its   09
applications-venturimeter, orificemeter, rotameter, pitot tube, Impulse-
Momentum equation and its applications, Reynolds Transport Theorem and
its application.
Dimensional Analysis: Secondary or derived quantities, Reyleigh method,
Buckingham−𝜋theorem, dimensionless numbers, Theory of similarity,
Model laws.
5   Laminar Flow: Navier-Stokes equation of motion, developing expression for   10
flow rate, pressure drop, shear stress, friction factor. Flow of viscous fluid in
circular pipes- Hagen Poiseuille law, Couette flow.
Turbulent Flow: Shear stresses in turbulent flow, theories of turbulent shear
stress, hydro-dynamically smooth and rough surface, modeling of
turbulence, Moody’s chart.
Flow Through pipes: Energy losses in pipes: Minor and Major losses, Darcy-
Weisbatch equation for head loss in pipes, hydraulic gradient lines, and total
energy lines, pipes in series and parallel, Equivalent pipe.
6   Boundary Layer Theory: Concept of Boundary layer, Boundary layer over   5
flat plate, Boundary Layer thickness, momentum thickness, displacement
thickness and energy thickness. Boundary layer equations and their
solutions. Blasius solution (without derivation), Von-Karman momentum
integral equation. Laminar boundary layer and turbulent boundary layer.
Separation and control and Concept of drag.

techniques. It equips the students with intermediate to advanced level concepts and tools in
probability and statistics that help them tackle relevant problems within engineering domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to

correlation and regression,

be performed on beams and power transmitting shafts. It develops the ability to assess the

Objectives
The course is aimed at imparting basic knowledge of science of materials and physical
metallurgy. This course introduces and cements the concept of structure property
correlations. It is designed to lay the foundation for the detailed understanding of
mechanical behavior of materials, phase diagrams, heat treatment and failure of
materials. The students are also introduced to certain applications of ferrous, non-
ferrous and new age materials.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to
1. Relate mechanical properties with the mechanical processing of materials,
2. Analyze the root cause of failure in different types of materials,
3. Recommend heat treatment processes with the help of phase diagrams,
4. Select appropriate materials for various applications depending on the structural
requirements,

plastic   deformation.   Deformation   in   single   crystal and
polycrystalline materials. Cold and Hot working of materials and
Strain hardening of metals. Recrystallization annealing, recovery and
grain growth.
2   Testing of Materials:   07

hardness testing, Impact testing.
Non-Destructive Testing: Dye Penetrant, magnetic particle and
ultrasonic testing.

and brittle fracture.

The course is aimed at developing the detailed understanding of various mechanism used
in devices or machines. This course focuses on analysis of the motion of mechanisms and to
design mechanisms that yield the desired motion. The course is designed for the students to

Course Objectives
The principal objective of this course is to provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of
living organisms from the perspective of engineers. To encourage engineering students to think about
solving biological problems with engineering tools. To make them aware of the application of
engineering principles in biology and engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.
Course Outcomes
After successful completion of the course, student would be able to
1. convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are
diverse,
2. identify and classify microorganisms while understanding molecular basis of DNA as a genetic
material for information transfer,
3. classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   3
Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as Mathematics, Physics
and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences between science and
engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and camera, Bird flying and
aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an independent scientific
discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss how biological observations
of 18th Century that lead to major discoveries. Examples from -Brownian motion
and the origin of thermodynamics by referring to the original observation of
Robert Brown and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight the fundamental
importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.
MBA(Tech)/Mechanical/Sem-IV/2021-22/Page 23
SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
2.   Classification
Convey that classification per se   is not what biology   is   all about.   6
The   underlying   criterion,   such   as   morphological,   biochemical   or
ecological   be   highlighted. Hierarchy   of   life   forms at
phenomenological   level. A common   thread weaves   this   hierarchy
Classification.Discuss classification based on   (a) cellularity-Unicellular or
multicellular (b) ultrastructure- prokaryotes or eucaryotes. (c) energy and Carbon
utilization -Autotrophs, heterotrophs, lithotropes (d) Ammonia excretion -
aminotelic, uricoteliec, ureotelic (e) Habitata- acquatic or terrestrial (e) Molecular
taxonomy- three major kingdoms of life. A given organism can come under
different category based on classification. Model organisms for the study of
biology come from different groups. E.coli, S.cerevisiae, D. Melanogaster, C.
elegance, A. Thaliana, M. musculus
3.   Genetics
Convey that "Genetics is to biology what Newton's laws are to Physical Sciences"   6
Mendel's laws, Concept of segregation and independent assortment. Concept of
allele. Gene mapping, Gene interaction, Epistasis. Meiosis and Mitosis be taught
as a part of genetics. Emphasis to be give not to the mechanics of cell division nor
the phases but how genetic material passes from parent to offspring. Concepts of
recessiveness and dominance. Concept of mapping of phenotype to genes.
Discuss about the single gene disorders in humans. Discuss the concept of
complementation using human genetics.
4.   Biomolecules   5
Convey that all forms of life has the same building blocks and yet the
manifestations are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of life. In this context
discuss monomeric units and polymeric structures. Discuss about sugars, starch
and cellulose. Amino acids and proteins. Nucleotides and DNA/RNA. Two
carbon units and lipids.
5.   Enzymes   5
Convey that without catalysis life would not have existed on earth Enzymology:
How to monitor enzyme catalyzed reactions. How does an enzyme catalyze
reactions. Enzyme classification. Mechanism of enzyme action. Discuss at least
two examples. Enzyme kinetics and kinetic- parameters. Why should we know
these parameters to understand biology? RNA catalysis.
6.   Information Transfer   6
The molecular basis of coding and decoding genetic information is universal
Molecular basis of information transfer. DNA as a genetic material. Hierarchy of
DNA structure- from single stranded to double helix to nucleosomes. Concept of
genetic code. Universality and degeneracy of genetic code. Define gene in terms
of complementation and recombination.
MBA(Tech)/Mechanical/Sem-IV/2021-22/Page 24
SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
7.   Macromolecular analysis   5
How to analyses biological processes at the reductionistic level Proteins- structure
and function. Hierarch in protein structure. Primary secondary, tertiary and
quaternary structure. Proteins as enzymes, transporters, receptors and structural
elements.
8.   Metabolism   5
The fundamental principles of energy transactions are the same in physical and
biological world. Thermodynamics as applied to biological systems. Exothermic
and endothermic versus endergonic and exergonic reactions. Concept of Keq and
its relation to standard free energy. Spontaneity. ATP as an energy currency. This
should include the breakdown of glucose to CO2 + H2O (Glycolysis and Krebs
cycle) and synthesis of glucose from CO2 and H2O (Photosynthesis). Energy
yielding and energy consuming reactions. Concept of Energy Charge.
9.   Microbiology   4
Concept of single celled organisms. Concept of species and strains. Identification
and classification of microorganisms. Microscopy. Ecological aspects of single
celled organisms. Sterilization and media compositions. Growth kinetics.
Total   45

relevant to the planning, design, and operations of manufacturing or service firms. This course
also develops an understanding about quality management practices in organizations that facilitate
organizational effectiveness.
Outcomes

in-time and MRP systems along with their limitations

Pre-requisite: Engineering Thermodynamics, Fluid Mechanics, Differential and Integral Calculus
Course Objective
This course is designed to provide knowledge of different modes of heat transfer with different laws
of conduction, convection and radiation. It also helps to provide understanding of different
applications of conduction, convection and radiation.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the basic laws of heat transfer
2. Analyse realistic problems involving different modes of heat transfer
3. Apply basic principles of heat transfer to design heat transfer devices
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Basic Concepts   15
Modes of Heat Transfer, its mechanism and mathematical models.
Conduction Heat Transfer
Fourier’s general conduction equation in Cartesian, Cylindrical and Spherical co-
ordinates (for cylindrical and spherical walls derivation of Fourier’s three-
dimensional equation is not included), thermal resistance, solution of Fourier’s
equation for one dimensional steady state heat conduction through various
configurations such as plane, cylindrical, spherical wall, composite medium.
Critical thickness of insulation and its importance.
Heat Transfer from Extended Surfaces
Types of fins, Governing equation, fin effectiveness, efficiency of fins, concept of
corrected fin length, application of fins.
Unsteady State Heat Conduction
Lumped System Analysis
2.   Convection Heat Transfer   15
Forced and natural convection, hydrodynamic and thermal boundary layer,
Convection heat transfer coefficient, Momentum and energy equation for laminar
boundary layer, Laminar and Turbulent flow, principles of dimensional analysis,
physical significance of dimensionless numbers, Nusselt number, Prandtl
number, Reynolds number, Grashof number.
Empirical relations and their use for forced internal and external convection for
circular and non-circular ducts.
Empirical relations and their use for free convection on vertical, horizontal flat
plate and cylinders.
Boiling and Condensation
Physical phenomenon and Pool boiling curve.
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
3.   Thermal Radiation   07
Introduction to physical mechanism, concept of black body, grey body and
radiation properties. Microwave Heating.
Basic laws of radiation; Planck’s law, Kirchoff’s law, Stefan-Boltzman law,
Wein’s-displacement law and Lambert’s Cosine law, Intensity of radiation,
radiosity, shape factor for simple geometries, heat exchange between non-black
bodies, Radiation Shield.
4.   Heat Exchangers   08
Classification, temperature distribution in parallel and counter flow
arrangement, overall heat transfer coefficient, fouling factor, log mean
temperature difference method, Effectiveness-NTU method.
Total   45

control the physical output work.

Course Objective
This course provides the understanding of the development and design aspects of products, impart
knowledge of business and technical concerns about the different methodologies of product
development. This course also discusses the concept of product life cycle and product data
management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1.   Identify the different stages of product development and design with modern approaches
2. Apply the knowledge of Technology Forecasting using S-Curve in product development as
per customers need
3. Describe the process of benchmarking of products, technologies & techniques product design
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration

Definition of product design, product development versus product design, types
of design and redesign, design by evolution and innovation, factors in product
design, morphology of product design (seven phases), standardization,
simplification and specialization in product design, product life cycle and its
various phases, modern approaches- concurrent design in product development,
product development team and product development planning with reference to
ISO standard, new product development process/stages, difference between
product verification and production validation.

Technology forecasting and Technology S-curve, Kano model, Mission statement
and technical questioning. Economic analysis of product, customer needs and
satisfaction, customer population and market segmentation, gathering customer
needs information, analysis of gathered information.

analysis, concept selection-design evaluation, estimation of technical feasibility,
concept selection process, Pugh’s concept, selection charts, numerical concept
scoring, process of concept embodiment, system modeling, Failure Mode Effect
Analysis (FMEA), functional modeling and decomposition, fast method, subtract
and operate procedure, establishing system functionality.

Engineering; Managing Competitiveness- benchmarking, outsourcing and mass
customization.

This course introduces the basic concepts of vibrations and discusses free vibration of an undamped
single-degree of-freedom system. This course also deals with two-degree-of-freedom systems, which
require two independent coordinates to describe their motion. The modeling of continuous
systems as multidegree-of-freedom systems is also presented in this course.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Derive the equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom system
2. Solve two-degree-of-freedom free- and forced-vibration problems
3. Formulate the equations of motion of multidegree-of-freedom systems

1.   Fundamentals of Vibration   07
Basic Concepts of Vibration, Classification of Vibration, Vibration Analysis
Procedure, Spring Elements, Mass or Inertia Elements, Damping Elements,
Harmonic Motion, Harmonic Analysis
2.   Single-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   08
Free Vibration of an Undamped Translational System, Free Vibration of an
Undamped Torsional System, Free Vibration with Viscous Damping, Free
Vibration with Coulomb Damping.
3.   Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   06
Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration, Free Vibration Analysis of an
Undamped System, Torsional System, Forced-Vibration Analysis.
4.   Multidegree-of-Freedom Systems   09
Modeling of Continuous Systems as Multi degree of Freedom Systems, Equations
of Motion, Influence Coefficients, Generalized Coordinates and Generalized
Forces, Lagrange s Equations, Equations of Motion of Undamped Systems in

Course Objective
The main purpose of this course is to introduce students with renewable energy resources
availability, potential and suitability as a substitute for conventional energy resources in future
energy demands.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify sustainable energy solutions for sustainable development
2. Analyze renewable energy resources availability and utilization
3. Demonstrate competency in renewable systems analysis independently
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   05
Renewable and non-renewable energy sources, global and Indian scenario.
Energy Alternatives
The solar option, nuclear option, tar sands and oil shale, tidal energy,
geothermal energy.
2.   Solar Energy   10
Solar radiation, availability, measurement and estimation, solar thermal
conversion devices such as flat plate collector, tubular collector, solar air
collector, solar concentrator and storage.
Applications
Crop drying, distillation, water heating, electric power generation.
Solar Photovoltaic
Photovoltaic   cell technologies, generations of solar   cell,   electrical
characteristics, photovoltaic module and array, photovoltaic module system
components and design.
3.   Biomass Energy Conversion   07
Biomass characteristics and their availability, biofuel production processes,
bio-methane, bio-hydrogen, alcoholic fermentation, biodiesel, microbial fuel
cell, biomass based steam power plant, combined cycle power plant,
cogeneration plant, Energy from Waste.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering

Wind turbines, aerodynamics, types of turbines wind energy conversion system,
wind turbine generator types, advantages and disadvantages.
Hydro Power
Water turbines, hydroelectric system theory, measurement and components,
advantages and disadvantages of hydroelectric system.
5.   Geothermal Energy   08
Structure of earth, geothermal resources, exploration of geothermal energy.
OTEC
Principle, applications.
Tidal
principle, power calculation, tidal modes of operation.
Wave
wave motion, energy conversion and devices applications.

Initial and annual costs, present worth calculation, annual savings, payback
period.

Course Objective
The objective of the course is to familiarize with basic knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. It teaches about various
additive manufacturing techniques.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   06
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.
2.   Classification of Additive Manufacturing Techniques   12
Material Extrusion:
Process mechanism, process parameters, extrusion of: ceramics, metals,
biomaterials, composites, contour crafting, concrete printing
Vat Polymerization:
Process mechanism, process parameters, advantages, disadvantages,
applications, Digital Light Processing (DLP), recent advances, Large-Scale
Rapid Liquid Printing.
Binder & material jetting processes:
Binder jettng process workflow, material requirements, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
Material Jetting process workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ.
Powder bed fusion AM process:
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
Selective laser sintering (SLS), process mechanism, process parameters,
selective laser melting (SLM), process workflow and material requirements,
powder melting mechanisms, electron beam melting (EBM) process.
Sheet Lamination AM Processes:
Process mechanism, process parameters, ultrasonic additive manufacturing
(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters
Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Processes:
Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net
Shaping) and wire, process parameters, cold spray.
3.   Post- Processing   04
Product quality evaluation, need for post-processing, support material
removal, surface finish improvement, aesthetic improvement, property
enhancements using non-thermal and thermal techniques.
4.   Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM)   04
Design guidelines: part orientation, support, geometry considerations, layer
thickness, part size, material consideration, residual stress, topology
optimization, case studies on design for AM.
5.   Applications of AM & Industry 4.0   04
Aerospace, biomedical, defence, automobile, rapid tooling, reverse
engineering, economic consideration, Industry 4.0 for AM, case studies on
application of AM in various industries.
Total   30

1. Gibson I, Rosen D W, Stucker B, Additive Manufacturing Technologies: Rapid Prototyping to Direct
Digital Manufacturing, 2nd Edition, Springer, 2015.

applications, 3D Hubs, 2017.

Course Objective
The principal objective of this course is to introduce basics of backend of drafting packages and
to give hands on experience on the 3D modeling software. The course has been structured to
impart knowledge of NC/CNC machines and programming of CNC using machine codes
along with providing concepts of GT, CAPP, CAQC and CIM.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Create accurate and precise geometry of complex engineering systems and use the
geometric models in different engineering applications
2. Apply the concepts of machining for the purpose of selection of machining parameters and
cutting tools for CNC milling and turning
3. Relate different CAD/CAM/CIM and various data management systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction and Elements of Interactive Computer Graphics   08
The design process, computers for design process, product life cycle and
CAD/CAM, concurrent engineering in product design and development,
collaborative engineering, CAD system architecture - software and
hardware, the role of modeling and communication, modeling using CAD
2.   Techniques for Geometric Modeling   06
Graphic standards, the parametric representation of geometry - Bezier
curves, cubic spline curve, B-spline curve, parametric representation of
line, circle, ellipse and parabola, constructive solid geometry (CSG),
boundary representation (B-rep), wire frame modeling, solid modeling,
surface modeling, feature based modeling, assembly modeling - different
approaches of creating an assembly, parent child relationship

2D and 3D transformations   (translation,   rotation, scaling and
magnification), concatenations, matrix representation, problems on
transformations. object transformation, mirror transformation, bill of
materials from attribute data, engineering data management system,
relational data base for design, object oriental database, design information
systems

Introduction, basic components of NC system, NC procedure, NC
coordinate systems, NC motion control systems, various actuation systems
and feedback devices like encoder, tachogenerator etc., applications,
advantages and disadvantages of NC machines, constructional details of
CNC machines, CNC programming concepts, manual part programming

Course Objective
This course is designed to impart knowledge of the principles and procedures for the design of
mechanical power transmission components. It also helps to understand the standard procedure
available for design of transmission of mechanical elements.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Articulate the design of belt drives and selection of belt, rope and chain drives
2. Analyze forces to design spur gears and helical gears
3. Design bevel and worm gears

Unit Description   Duration

hoisting wire ropes and pulleys

Fatigue strength, Factor of safety, Gear materials, Design of straight tooth spur &
helical gears based on strength and wear considerations, Pressure angle in the
normal and transverse plane, Equivalent number of teeth-forces for helical gears.

of teeth. Estimating the dimensions of pair of straight bevel gears. Worm Gear:

Pre-requisite: Basic Electrical Engineering, Engineering Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to wind energy and wind turbines. It introduces the current
challenges in modern wind turbine analysis, design, and development and provides a comprehensive
examination of state-of-the-art technologies.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Categorize various types of wind turbines and its principal components
2. Determine the mechanical power, types of stresses and the control parameters
3. Analyze the economics, effects on the environment, safety in operation and the potential hazards
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   10
Importance of renewable, technical issues, wind farm development, wind turbine
siting, new and future technologies, energy in a moving object and moving fluid,
power in the wind, power absorption by a turbine, wind speed variation, force
from wind, aerodynamic force, lift and drag coefficients, airfoils.
2.   Types and Components of Wind Turbine   10
Turbine classification, propeller wind turbine, The H-rotor, Darrieus turbine,
Savonius rotor, mechanical components - tower, foundation, rotor, nacelle,
gearbox, turbine brake, electrical components - generators, transformers and
anemometer.
3.   Propeller   05
Mechanical power, diagrams, mechanical power in a turbine, turbine power
variation with angular speed, daily energy production by a turbine, annual energy
production.
4.   Wind Turbine Design   10
Power accord with the wind speed, wind speed measurement, power calculations,
output power quality and requirement, blade pitch control, turbine operating
power curve, yaw control, parking brake, fault control, various operational states
of a turbine, loads on the rotor, aerodynamic loads on the blade, other blade loads,
vibrations, blade fatigue, blade construction.
MBA Tech/Mechanical/Sem-VII/2023-24/Page 7
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
5.   Economics, Environmental Concerns and Safety   10
Fundamentals of economics, initial costs of a wind energy project, operating cost,
comparison with other energy sources, cost per unit, onshore wind farms, noise,
view, landscape, effects on birds, RF interference and effect on communications,
offshore wind farms, effects on birds and marine animals, safety and working
with wind turbines, effect of temperature and environmental changes, protection
from lightning, ice forming on the blades, wind energy in urban areas, working
environment, possible hazards, commonsense safety rules, standardized safety
rules, and official regulations, climbing gear, minimizing the risk .
Total   45

Objectives:

 To determine the failure criteria of a body subjected to various stresses

performed on materials
Outcomes:

Unit Description   Duration

bulk modulus, yield stress, ultimate stress, factor of safety, shear stress,

bending moment diagrams for statically determinate beams for
different types of loading.

problems involving application of flexure formula, section modulus,
moment of resistance of a section.

sections used commonly for structural purposes.

and parallel).

members subjected to eccentric loads, core of a section, problems on
chimneys involving lateral loads.

stress on an oblique plane of a member subjected to General two   5
directional stress systems. Principal planes and principal stresses,
maximum shear stress Mohr’s circle concept.
6   Deflection of Beams: Deflection of cantilevers, simply supported and
overhanging beams using double integration and Macaulay’s methods   5
for different types of loading.

Pre-requisite: Mathematics   III (MBME03007) &   Engineering Mechanics
(MBME03012)
Objectives:
 To develop a fundamental in analytical and practical Fluid mechanics.
 To impart knowledge of different types of fluid flows and boundary layers
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Understand the fluid properties, their static- dynamic nature and the
concepts of viscous boundary layers.
 Analyze fundamental behavior of incompressible fluids.
 Apply fluid mechanics concepts to solve real life problems.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1   Fluid Properties: Concept of continuum, fluid properties,   3
Classification of fluid, Newton’s law of viscosity, stress-strain
relationship.
2   Fluid Statics: Basic hydrostatic equation, Pascal’s Law,   10
application to Manometers and mechanical gauges, hydrostatic
forces on plane and curved submerged surfaces.
Buoyancy and Floatation: Archimedes’ Principle, buoyancy
force and centre of buoyancy, metacentre, metacentric height,
analytical method to find metacentric height, condition of
equilibrium of submerged bodies, oscillation of a floating body
3   Fluid Kinematics: Description of fluid motion-Lagrangian   8
method and Euler’s method, classification of flow types- steady
and unsteady, uniform and non-uniform, laminar and turbulent,
one two and three- dimensional flow, rotational and irrotational,
laminar and turbulent, compressible and incompressible.
Flow patterns- stream lines, path lines, stream tubes and streak
lines. Continuity equation (Cartesian and polar co-ordinates),
circulation and vorticity, velocity potential and stream function.
4   Fluid Dynamics: Euler’s equation of motion, Bernoulli’s   9
equation and   its   applications-venturimeter,   orificemeter,
rotameter, pitot tube, Impulse-Momentum equation and its

applications, Reynolds Transport Theorem and its application.
Dimensional Analysis: Secondary or derived quantities,
Reyleigh method, Buckingham−𝜋theorem,   dimensionless
numbers, Theory of similarity, Model laws.
5   Laminar Flow: Navier-Stokes equation of motion, developing   10
expression for flow rate, pressure drop, shear stress, friction
factor. Flow of viscous fluid in circular pipes- Hagen Poiseuille
law, Couette flow.
Turbulent Flow: Shear stresses in turbulent flow, theories of
turbulent shear stress, hydro-dynamically smooth and rough
surface, modeling of turbulence, Moody’s chart.
Flow Through pipes: Energy losses in pipes: Minor and Major
losses, Darcy-Weisbatch equation for head loss in pipes,
hydraulic gradient lines, and total energy lines, pipes in series
and parallel, Equivalent pipe.
6 Boundary Layer Theory: Concept of Boundary layer, Boundary   5
layer over flat plate, Boundary Layer thickness, momentum
thickness, displacement thickness and energy thickness.
Boundary layer equations and their solutions. Blasius solution
(without   derivation), Von-Karman momentum   integral
equation. Laminar boundary layer and turbulent boundary
layer. Separation and control and Concept of drag.
Total   45

capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industry.
● To get acquainted with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of Additive Manufacturing.
● To explore the Design for Additive Manufacturing capabilities of each AM process and

Pre-requisite: Machine Drawing (MBME03008), Design of Machine Elements - I

Objectives:
 To understand the design of gears and gear systems used in the industry
 To provide the knowledge of different types of bearings and their selection
 To introduce concept of robust design
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Select appropriate gears for power transmission on the basis of given load and speed
 Design gears and bearings based on given conditions
 Select bearing for a given application from manufacturing catalogues
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
12
1   Gear Design: Types of gear and its applications, selection of gear
materials with desirable properties, modes of Gear tooth failure and
methods of gear lubrication
Spur Gear: Terminology, minimum number of teeth, face width and
module relation, force analysis, beam strength of gear tooth (Lewis
Equation), Velocity factor, service factor, effective load on gear tooth,
Wear Strength of gear tooth (Buckingham Equation), Module
calculation based on beam and wear strength.
Helical   Gear: Terminology, transverse and   normal module,
Virtual number of teeth, tooth proportions, force analysis, beam and
wear strength, effective load on gear tooth.
11
2   Bevel Gears: Types of Bevel gears, terminology of straight tooth
bevel gear, formative number of teeth, force analysis, beam and
wear strength, dynamic load and effective load, materials
selection for straight bevel gear, introduction to spiral bevel gear.
Worm Gear: Terminology, geometric proportions of worm gears,
force analysis, friction in worm gears, efficiency of worm gears,
material selection, strength rating of worm gears, wear rating of
worm gears, thermal considerations.

Pre-requisite: All Mechanical Engineering subjects till semester VI
Objectives:
To inculcate the ability to gather relevant information and evaluate the feasibility of the
project presenting it in the form of report.
Outcomes :
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Apply knowledge of Mechanical Engineering for problem identification.
 Analyze literature for feasibility study of the topic chosen.
 Develop and evaluate solutions for defined problem.
 Present the proposed methodology with report.
Detailed Syllabus:
A group of 3-4 students will select a topic in the area of Mechanical engineering. The
students and faculty mentor will decide the topic. The students will study literature
related to the topic. After literature survey, problem definition and methodology should
be finalized.
Internet References: As prescribed by Faculty
Detail guidelines for the project:
Project – Part- I Activities to be done:
1. The Project group to be formed consisting of not more than 4 students.
2. The project area and topic is to be selected in consultation with faculty mentors,
alternatively students can propose the topics.
3. The names of the students and the topic of the project is to be submitted in the first
week of Semester along with name of the Mentor.
4. The first phase of the project will involve Literature Survey and feasibility study.
5. Student is required to submit a 1-2 pages weekly report on the work done to the
Mentor. Attendance will be given on the report. There would be continuous
evaluation based on the weekly report submitted for 50 marks.
6. Report primarily containing Literature Survey and feasibility study is to be submitted
at the end of the Semester. (Spiral Bound Report)
7. Presentation (About 30 minutes) of the work done during the Semester to be
evaluated by Internal Examiner and faculty mentor.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Thermodynamics (MBME04010), Thermal Engineering
(BTME04011), Heat Transfer (BTME06001)
Objectives:
 To provide knowledge of combustion process in I.C Engines.
 To study the various conventional and alternative fuels with their performance on I.C
Engines.
 To provide the knowledge for modern trends in I.C engines, emission standards and
pollution control measures.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Understand the combustion process in I.C Engines.
 Analyze different electronic fuel injection system, supercharging and its effect on
performance of SI and CI engine.
 Interpret different alternative fuels and its emissions, then the method to control these
emissions.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan )
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Types of I. C. Engines: Two stroke four stroke (S.I. and C.I.) engines,   3
engine working principle and valve timing and port timing diagram.
2   Engine performance test: purpose and types, measurement of power,   10
Engine system and performance parameters evaluation, theory of
combustion, principle of combustion, S.I. and C.I. engine combustion
processes and parameters, and its dependence on engine variables.
3   Combustion: adiabatic flame temperature, combustion processes and   10
combustion chambers for SI and CI engines, pollutant formation and
control, effect of engine variables on combustion processes, knocking in
SI and CI engines, petroleum-based fuels, gasoline & diesel fuel and their
properties, blending, knock rating of engine fuels.
4   Carburation: working principles, chemically correct air-fuel ratio and   11
load variation, Carburetors & modern air fuel systems, compensating
devices, venturi and jet dimension calculation, injection system, super
charging, engine lubrication and cooling.

Engines, Alternate fuels like alcohol, hydrogen, natural gas & liquefied
petroleum gas; suitability, engine modifications, merits and demerits as
IC engine fuels.
5   Advances in I.C Engines: Stratified charge spark ignition engine, lean   11
burn engine, dual fuel engine, multi point fuel injection gasoline engine,
homogeneous charge compression ignition engine, plasma ignition,
electric / hybrid vehicles. Pollutant formation and control, emission
standards, pollution monitoring instruments and techniques, control
measures such as DOC, DPF, SCR and LNT.

Pre-requisite: Fluid Mechanics (BTME04010), Heat Transfer (BTME06001)
Objectives:
 To provide the understanding of basics of CFD and application perspective
 To know numerical techniques of discretization and solving linear algebraic and PDE
equations
 To introduce techniques to solve problems related to heat transfer and fluid flow
Outcomes:
After successful completion of the course, students should be able to
 Understand the basics of CFD and working of CFD software and their solution
methodology.
 Analyze the discretized equations for solving heat transfer and fluid flow problems.
 Apply numerical techniques for addressing the problems related to heat transfer,
fluid flow, convection and diffusion.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan )
Unit Description   Duration
1   Introduction to CFD: scope and application of CFD, methods of   3
predictions like experimental, theoretical working of commercial CFD
software, solution methodology- preprocessing, solver, post processing.
2   Mathematical description of Fluid Flow: Concept of mathematical   8
modeling,   Basic   conservation   equation   (continuity   equation,
momentum equation, energy Equation) in differential and Integral form.
Initial and Boundary Conditions, Initial and Boundary Value problems.
One-dimensional computations by Finite Difference, Finite Element and
Finite Volume methods.
3   Grid Generation and Discretization Methods:   Structured and   8
unstructured Grids,   O-type, H-type, C-type of Structured Grid
Generation, Mesh Adaptation, The Nature of Numerical Methods, The
Discretization Concept, The Structure of the Discretization Equation,
Methods of Deriving the Discretization Equations, Taylor-Series
Formulation, Variational Formulation, Method of Weighted Residuals,
Control Volume Formulation.

method with Gausian Elimination; Parabolic Equations – Explicit
Schemes and Von Neumann Stability Analysis, Implicit Schemes.
5   Application of CFD to Heat Flow:   6
Steady One and two dimensional conduction, Unsteady One and two
dimensional conduction, Over relaxation and Under relaxation
6   Application of CFD to Convection and Diffusion:   6
Steady One-dimensional and Two Dimensional Convection-Diffusion,
Unsteady One and two dimensional Convection-Diffusion
7   Application of CFD to Incompressible Fluid Flow: Governing   6
Equations, Stream Function-Vorticity Method, Determination of
Pressure for Viscous Flow, The SIMPLE, SIMPLER Algorithm,
Introduction to Turbulence Modeling, Basic Theories of Turbulence.

Pre-requisite: Fundamental Knowledge of physics, chemistry and mathematics.

Objectives:
1, To provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living organisms
from the perspective of engineers.
2. To encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems
with engineering tools.

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to :
1. Convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the
manifestations are diverse.
2, Identify DNA asa genetic material in the molecular basis of information transfer.
3. Classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme
action.
4. Apply thermodynamic principles to biological systems.
5. Identify and classify microorganisms.
Detailed Syllabus: ( per session plan )

Unit | Description Duration
1. Introduction 3
Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as
Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental
differences between science and engineering by drawing a
comparison between eye and camera, Bird flying and aircraft.
Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an independent
scientific discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss how
biological observations of 18th Century that lead to major
discoveries. Examples from Brownian motion and the origin of
thermodynamics by referring to the original observation of Robert
Brown and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight the

fundamental importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.

Model organisms for the study of biology come from different

Convey that “Genetics is to biology what Newton’s laws are to

nor the phases but how genetic material passes from parent to
offspring. Concepts of recessiveness and dominance. Concept of
mapping of phenotype to genes. Discuss about the single gene
disorders in humans.
Discuss the concept of complementation using human genetics.

Convey that all forms of life has the same building blocks and yet
the manifestations are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes - I (MBME03009)
Objectives:
 To introduce various approaches to productivity.
 To impart knowledge of work-study techniques for examination of human work.
 To apply ergonomic principles to enable working effectively with minimization of
occupational stresses.
 To introduce the concept of value engineering and applications.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Calculate the productivity of resources for improvements.
 Improve the methods to measure parameters such as time and magnitude of
activities performed.
 Assess the cost effectiveness of each function of the product in terms of usefulness to
the customer.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1   Productivity: Productivity concepts. Analysing the work content of a   06
job to identify and reduce/eliminate the excess work content.
Interdependence between working conditions and productivity.
Significance of theory of Scientific Management. Improving Efficiency
and Productivity through Work study. Work study components.
Relationship between Method Study and Time Study.
2   Method Study: Basic procedure of method study. Factors in selecting a   08
job to a studied. Recording the facts with charts and diagrams.
Questioning technique for development of new method. Role of
Management and workers in implementation.
3   Facilities & Workplace Design: Aligning the physical facilities- plant   05
layout, equipment and work flow as per the production processes.
Prinicples of Motion Economy. Standardisation of the process.

work measurement. Need of work sampling technique. Conducting
work sampling study. Analytical estimation of work. Concept of
rating factor. Consideration of various allowances. Standard time for
work. Predetermined time standards. Use standard data. MOST for
work measurement. Use of time standards.
5   Ergonomics: Field of Ergonomics. Physical and cognitive issues of   07
ergonomics. Aims of ergonomics considerations. Working postures of
operatives.   Design   of   objects,   facilities and   environment.
Anthropometrical details. Database of human factors. Ergonomic
improvement of physical and cognitive issues. Ergonomics principals.
Information input and human control of systems. Work space and
arrangement. Living environment. Visual displays

control function of production at middle and operational level.
 To focus on functions for estimation and allocation of resources
 To impart knowledge of procedures for meeting production and inventory
targets in production organizations covering a wide range product types
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 To develop an understanding of the short and medium term planning and control
function of production at middle and operational level
 Analyze   planning,   professional and   engineering   decisions within a
manufacturing environment
 To focus on functions for estimation and allocation of resources
 To impart knowledge of procedures for meeting production and inventory
targets in production organizations covering a wide range product types

1   Fundamentals of Manufacturing: Manufacturing definition, value   8
adding conversion process, resources and optimum allocation;
functions of production; Production Planning and Control and its
interrelationship with other functions such as marketing, finance,
R&D organization for production systems; job order, batch
production.
2   Economic Analysis: Factors to be considered in product design.   7
Economics of scales fixed Cost, variable cost, break even chart, P-V
chart, multiple product P-V charts, and make-buy decision.
3   Plant Location and Plant Layout: Factors to be considered in plant   6

Objectives:
 To understand the design of gears and gear systems used in the industry
 To provide the knowledge of different types of bearings and their selection
 To introduce concept of robust design
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Select appropriate gears for power transmission on the basis of given load and speed
 Design gears and bearings based on given conditions
 Select bearing for a given application from manufacturing catalogues
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
12
1   Gear Design: Types of gear and its applications, selection of gear
materials with desirable properties, modes of Gear tooth failure and
methods of gear lubrication
Spur Gear: Terminology, minimum number of teeth, face width and
module relation, force analysis, beam strength of gear tooth (Lewis
Equation), Velocity factor, service factor, effective load on gear tooth,
Wear Strength of gear tooth (Buckingham Equation), Module
calculation based on beam and wear strength.
Helical   Gear: Terminology, transverse and   normal module,
Virtual number of teeth, tooth proportions, force analysis, beam and
wear strength, effective load on gear tooth.
11

bevel gear, formative number of teeth, force analysis, beam and
wear strength, dynamic load and effective load, materials
selection for straight bevel gear, introduction to spiral bevel gear.
Worm Gear: Terminology, geometric proportions of worm gears,
force analysis, friction in worm gears, efficiency of worm gears,
material selection, strength rating of worm gears, wear rating of
worm gears, thermal considerations.

 To understand basic elements of robots through mathematical modelling.
 To analyze motion control aspects of robotics.

Outcomes:

 Model simple and reasonably challenging robots using differential equations
 Understand the basic motion control algorithms used in robotics
 Develop an understanding of the software aspects in contemporary robotics
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1   Fundamentals of Robotics: DC motor modeling, gearbox, rack and   10
pinion, power screw, timing belt drive models, Fundamentals of
motion, desired motion design, motion planning.

for motion control.

robots, 2D Cartesian robot, 2D polar robot, differential robot, geared
wrists and grippers.
4   Analysis of Robots: Grubler-Kutzbach criterion, Denavit-Hartneberg   8
classic algorithm for reference frames, Homogeneous Coordinate
Transformation, the Homogeneous Coordinate Transformation
Matrix, the arm matrix.
5   Kinetics of Robots: Tool-configuration Jacobian matrix, Manipulator   3
Jacobian Matrix and their utility.
6   Dynamic Modelling: Robot dynamics, Hamilton’s   principle,   8
Lagrange’s equations, Virtual Work done by non-conservative forces,
equations of motion.
7   Modeling and Simulation: SCARA Robot, deriving equations of   4
motion, Simulation of equations of motion for relevant robots.
